docs.title: The territory: from market stall to mid-corporate
docs.where: Module 00 · What Business Banking Actually Is
docs.text: Start with the population, because the population is the problem. At the start of 2025 the UK had roughly 5.7 million private sector businesses, and 5.68 million of them — 99.85% — were SMEs . Around 56% of the total were sole traders , and about three quarters of those employ nobody but the owner. Collectively, SMEs employ roughly 16.9 million people and turn over about £2.8 trillion a year. That is the raw material of a Business Banking book: not a smooth continuum of similar borrowers, but a pyramid with an enormous base of one-person firms, a middle of employing small businesses, and a thin apex of small corporates with finance directors and audited accounts. Business Banking — BB, in the internal shorthand you will now live inside — is the stretch of the bank that serves this pyramid, from the newly registered window cleaner to the £6m-turnover engineering firm. Below it sits Retail, which you know: homogeneous products sold to individuals. Above it sits Corporate and, further up, Investment Banking: bespoke facilities for firms large enough to negotiate. BB is the awkward middle. Its customers are legally businesses but often economically households — the director's mortgage, the personal guarantee , and the company overdraft are frequently the same balance sheet wearing three hats. The consequence, and the theme of this entire atlas, is heterogeneity. A cards portfolio contains a million accounts that differ in degree. A BB portfolio contains a café, a haulage contract

docs.title: Where the banks draw the lines
docs.where: Module 00 · What Business Banking Actually Is
docs.text: There is no statutory definition of Business Banking. Each bank cuts the pyramid where it likes, almost always on annual turnover — turnover segmentation — because turnover is observable, roughly tracks complexity, and determines how much manual underwriting a relationship can economically justify. At Barclays, the line sits at £6.5m: Business Banking, housed within Barclays UK , serves everything from start-ups to firms with up to £6.5m annual turnover, while the UK Corporate Bank — carved out as a distinct division in the 2024 reorganisation — takes businesses above £6.5m through to FTSE 350 names. Lloyds slices twice: small business accounts below £3m turnover, a business tier from £3m to £25m, and Commercial Banking above £25m. NatWest draws its retail-adjacent line lower still, keeping firms up to roughly £2m turnover in its business banking segment before they graduate to Commercial & Institutional. Same country, same borrowers, boundaries ranging from £2m to £25m. This matters more than it looks. When an analyst compares SME coverage ratios across UK banks, they are rarely comparing like with like: one bank's "business banking" book is another's commercial mid-market. Barclays' £6.5m boundary means its BB book skews small — heavy in sole traders and micro-companies, lighter in the £10m–£25m firms that sit in Lloyds' equivalent segment. docs.title: The anchor product: the current account and the money that moves
docs.where: Module 00 · What Business Banking Actually Is
docs.text: The commercial heart of BB is not a loan. It is the business current account — the BCA — through which a firm's entire financial life flows: customer receipts, supplier payments, wages, VAT, the director's ill-advised drawings. Banks fight for BCAs because the account brings cheap deposits, fee income, and the first call on every subsequent product the business ever needs. In BB, deposits typically dwarf lending; the segment is structurally a deposit franchise with a loan book attached. Around the BCA cluster the transactional products. Merchant acquiring — card payment processing, at Barclays the domain of Barclaycard Payments — earns a slice of every card transaction and carries a subtle credit exposure: if a merchant fails after taking payment but before delivering (think tour operators), chargebacks land on the acquirer. FX services serve importers and exporters, mostly spot and simple forwards; the credit risk is settlement risk, small but real. Deposit products — instant access, notice, fixed term — carry no credit risk at all, but they fund the book and anchor the relationship. For you, the BCA's real treasure is informational. The turnover passing through the account — BCA turnover — is a live, unfalsifiable read on trading health, months ahead of any filed accounts. Falling receipts, rising reliance on the overdraft ceiling, bounced direct debits: this is the raw feed of behavioural scoring in BB, doing the job the credit bureau did for you in cards. docs.title: The lending shelf: five products, five risk shapes
docs.where: Module 00 · What Business Banking Actually Is
docs.text: BB lending is a shelf of five basic products, and each has a distinct risk anatomy — a different dominant parameter among PD , LGD and EAD . The overdraft is working-capital oxygen: a revolving limit on the BCA, repayable on demand, usually unsecured or floating-charge secured at the small end. Its risk is EAD-shaped. A healthy firm touches its limit occasionally; a dying one lives at the ceiling and pushes through it. Utilisation rises precisely as PD rises — the credit-conversion problem you know from cards, sharpened. The term loan is the workhorse: a fixed advance amortising over one to ten-plus years, for expansion, acquisition or refinancing. EAD is predictable; the game is PD — will the cash flows survive the term? — and, where unsecured, LGD is brutal. The commercial mortgage lends against trading premises or investment property over 15–25 years. Superficially it rhymes with your old world; actually LGD rides the commercial property cycle, which is more violent and less liquid than residential, and tenant covenants can matter as much as the borrower. Asset finance — hire purchase and leasing — funds vehicles, plant and equipment, with the asset itself as security and often title retained by the bank. LGD is a used-asset resale question: a tipper truck holds value; bespoke software-laden machinery does not. "Hard" versus "soft" assets is the whole game. Invoice finance advances perhaps 80–90% against unpaid trade invoices. It is self-liquidating — customers' payments r

docs.title: Neither retail nor corporate
docs.where: Module 00 · What Business Banking Actually Is
docs.text: Underwriting first. Retail credit is statistical: bureau score, affordability calculation, automated decision, millions of times. Corporate credit is forensic: audited accounts, sector analysis, a credit paper argued before a sanctioning committee. BB is the hybrid — auto-decisioned at the small end using bureau-plus-behavioural data, manually underwritten above a threshold, with relationship lending surviving in the middle: a business manager covering hundreds of firms, knowing perhaps a tenth of them well. Data second, and this is the cultural shock. In cards you enjoyed deep bureau histories refreshed monthly. A BB underwriter faces filleted small-company accounts filed at Companies House up to nine months late — micro-entities need file little more than an abridged balance sheet — plus commercial bureau data that is thinner and staler than its consumer cousin. Hence the reliance on BCA behaviour, and increasingly on Open Banking feeds for non-customers. Security third. Retail lending is either cleanly secured (the mortgage) or cleanly unsecured (the card). BB security is baroque: personal guarantees that pierce the limited-liability veil, debentures granting fixed and floating charges over everything the company owns, title retained on financed assets. Recovery is a legal process with a timetable measured in years. Capital last. Smaller SME exposures can qualify for retail treatment under the capital rules, larger ones are corporate SME, and the SME supporting factor disc

docs.title: Why SME books misbehave
docs.where: Module 00 · What Business Banking Actually Is
docs.text: Take the retail modeller's three comforts — homogeneity, rich data, smooth losses — and remove each in turn. Heterogeneity first. The café and the haulier share a PD segment but not a failure mode: one dies of footfall, the other of fuel prices and a lost contract. Segment finely enough to be homogeneous and your buckets hold too few firms to calibrate; segment coarsely enough to calibrate and your buckets are zoos. There is no clean answer, only a managed trade-off. Data second. With thin bureau coverage and stale filed accounts, models lean on behavioural signals — above all BCA turnover . Powerful, but noisy and endogenous: a firm can slash costs, or quietly route receipts through a Starling account, and your signal degrades. Noisy inputs mean noisier PD , which means staging decisions — and therefore lifetime-loss recognition — sit on softer foundations than you are used to. Losses third. Retail losses arrive as drizzle; SME losses arrive as weather. Default frequency is low most years — the classic low-default portfolio problem — then insolvency cycles bite: 2025 saw 23,938 company insolvencies in England and Wales, around 77% of them creditors' voluntary liquidations , easing from 2023's thirty-year high. And single names matter: one £3m exposure gone bad moves a month's charge in a way no cards account ever could. Then there is what stands behind the loss. docs.title: Where you sit, and why the number moves
docs.where: Module 00 · What Business Banking Actually Is
docs.text: The BB impairment team sits where you'd expect — in the risk and finance machinery, between the credit-risk modellers who build PD/LGD/EAD and the financial reporting line that signs the ECL number into the accounts. What changes is the shape of the work. A BB book runs a split you rarely saw in cards: the mass of small exposures flows through collective assessment on modelled parameters, while larger or watchlisted names are individually assessed — a human builds discounted recovery cash flows, weighs the security, argues the case. Deciding which names cross that line, and challenging the workouts once they do, is a core discipline of the job. Now assemble the domino chain this module has been building. SME heterogeneity forces coarse segmentation; thin bureau data forces reliance on behavioural and BCA-turnover signals; noisy signals produce noisy PDs; noisy PDs make staging twitchy, swinging exposures between 12-month and lifetime loss; the collective/individual split adds step-changes whenever a big name migrates; and the sum is coverage volatility — a P&L charge that lurches in ways a mortgage book never would. Management papers over the gaps with PMAs , judgemental overlays that in SME portfolios can rival the modelled number itself. For scale: Barclays' group loan loss rate ran at 52bps for full-year 2025, comfortably within its through-the-cycle range — but the BB line beneath such group figures moves with insolvency weather the way cards never did. docs.title: Quakers, goldsmiths, and the original business bank
docs.where: Module 01 · History & Evolution of UK Business Banking
docs.text: Barclays begins, in 1690, as a business bank. John Freame and Thomas Gould — two Quaker goldsmith bankers — set up in Lombard Street taking deposits and making advances against the trade of the City. There was no retail franchise to speak of; the customer was the merchant, and the product was working capital. The partnership became one of the most successful of the early private banks and is generally credited as a pioneer of re-discounting bills of exchange sent up by provincial bankers — in modern language, buying short-dated trade receivables at a discount. That is invoice finance with a powdered wig on. The Quaker network mattered as much as the balance sheet. The Society of Friends was a closed community with severe internal sanctions for default — a Quaker who failed his creditors could be disowned by his meeting. Freame and Gould financed Quaker traders in the American colonies and the Caribbean, held the Society's central funds, and lent into Quaker-dominated ventures like the London Lead Company. Membership functioned as a credit bureau, a covenant package and a collections department in one. James Barclay, who married into the firm in 1736, gave it the name; the underwriting logic — lend to people whose character and cash flows you can observe closely — survived as what the literature now calls relationship lending . Two things from this era echo through everything that follows. First, UK business banking's historical strength was trade finance: short, self-liquidat

docs.title: The cartel century: an oligopoly rations credit
docs.where: Module 01 · History & Evolution of UK Business Banking
docs.text: Through the nineteenth century, hundreds of private and country banks amalgamated into a handful of joint-stock giants that settled with each other through the London Clearing House — the clearing banks . Barclay & Company Ltd was itself assembled in 1896 from a score of Quaker-linked private banks. By the early twentieth century a Big Five (later Big Four) dominated England and Wales, and they behaved less like competitors than like a public utility with shareholders: an interest-rate cartel fixed deposit rates by agreement, and lending rates moved in lockstep with Bank Rate. What changed for the SME borrower was the supply mechanism. From the 1930s, and formally through the post-war decades, the authorities managed credit by instruction: quantitative lending ceilings, directional guidance favouring exports and industry, and moral suasion from the Bank of England. When credit is rationed by decree, the marginal borrower is simply refused — and the marginal borrower was almost always the small firm without collateral or connections. The Macmillan Committee had already named the structural failure in 1931: a persistent shortfall in long-term finance for small companies, the Macmillan gap , which every subsequent decade rediscovers under a new brand. What losses followed? Almost none — and that is the trap. Rationed lending to the safest borrowers produced decades of negligible write-offs, which taught the clearers that business lending was intrinsically low-risk rather tha

docs.title: 1971: Competition and Credit Control lights the fuse
docs.where: Module 01 · History & Evolution of UK Business Banking
docs.text: In September 1971 the Bank of England replaced the entire apparatus with Competition and Credit Control : the clearing-bank cartel was dismantled, quantitative lending ceilings were abolished, and credit was henceforth to be controlled through price — interest rates and calls for special deposits — rather than administrative rationing. What changed: for the first time in a generation, banks could lend as much as they liked to whomever they liked. What it did to credit supply was immediate and violent. Broad money grew roughly 72 per cent between 1971 and the policy's effective abandonment in December 1973 — the Barber boom. The frothiest expansion came not from the clearers but from the fringe: lightly supervised secondary banks funding themselves in the new wholesale markets and lending against commercial property. Bank lending to property rose more than eight-fold between 1970 and 1974, with the secondary banks overtaking the clearing banks as the principal property lenders. This is the recurring UK pattern in its purest form: liberalise supply, and the marginal credit flows to property, because property is the collateral everyone believes in. What losses followed: the 1973 oil shock, a Minimum Lending Rate of 13 per cent, and a commercial property crash took the funding away and the collateral with it. Wholesale depositors ran from the secondary banks; from December 1973 the Bank of England corralled the clearers into the Lifeboat , a support pool that ultimately extended

docs.title: Big Bang 1986: the side-effects reach the business bank
docs.where: Module 01 · History & Evolution of UK Business Banking
docs.text: The Big Bang of 27 October 1986 deregulated the London Stock Exchange — fixed commissions abolished, the broker/jobber distinction ended, ownership opened to outsiders, trading moved onto screens. On its face this had nothing to do with lending to a haulier in Dudley. The effects arrived anyway, through three side doors. First, the clearers bought their way into securities. Barclays merged broker de Zoete & Bevan with jobber Wedd Durlacher to create BZW , and for the next decade board attention, capital and the most ambitious talent migrated toward investment banking. Business banking became the unglamorous utility that funded the adventure. Second, disintermediation: large corporates could increasingly fund themselves in the capital markets Big Bang supercharged, so the clearers' corporate lending margins thinned and the banks pushed down-market — into mid-corporates, SMEs and, fatally, commercial property — in search of yield. Third, the deregulatory temper of the age, amplified by the Lawson boom and financial liberalisation, produced a late-1980s surge in bank credit to exactly the sectors that would fail first. What it did to SME credit supply: more of it, cheaper, faster, and increasingly secured on the one asset class — property — whose price the lending itself was inflating. What losses followed belongs to the next section, because the bill arrived in 1990.

docs.title: The early-1990s recession: scar tissue that never faded
docs.where: Module 01 · History & Evolution of UK Business Banking
docs.text: Policy drove Bank Rate to 15 per cent in 1989–90 and held it high to defend sterling's ERM parity. Commercial and residential property values fell hard, and the SME book built in the boom failed in bulk: company liquidations in England and Wales roughly doubled from the late-1980s trough to a peak of around 24,000 a year in 1992, with unincorporated business failures on top. The parallel small banks crisis — within three years of BCCI's July 1991 closure, a quarter of the UK's small and medium-sized banks had failed — showed the funding side of the same storm, and the Bank of England again provided quiet liquidity support to stop contagion reaching the clearers. The mechanism that turned recession into rupture was the overdraft culture . UK SME borrowing was dominated by the on-demand overdraft , secured by an all-monies charge over the proprietor's home and a personal guarantee . On-demand means exactly that: as conditions deteriorated, banks cut limits and called facilities at the point of maximum borrower distress — procyclical deleveraging executed one phone call at a time. Businesses that were trading through the downturn were tipped into failure by the withdrawal of the facility itself; homes pledged as collateral were repossessed into a falling market. What losses followed: heavy write-offs across the clearers' business books, and something more durable — a rupture of trust between banks and small firms that produced parliamentary inquiries, codes of practice, and a ge

docs.title: Demutualisation and the last consolidation of the clearers
docs.where: Module 01 · History & Evolution of UK Business Banking
docs.text: The 1990s reshaped the register without reshaping the market. Demutualisation turned the great building societies into banks — Abbey National in 1989, then Halifax, Woolwich, Alliance & Leicester and Northern Rock in the class of 1997 — but these were mortgage machines with no SME franchise, no business current account capability and no branch-based relationship managers. They added ferocious competition to home loans and savings while leaving business banking untouched. Meanwhile the clearers themselves consolidated. Lloyds absorbed TSB in 1995; the Royal Bank of Scotland won the hostile contest for NatWest in 2000; Barclays bought the demutualised Woolwich the same year. Each deal was rational on cost grounds, and each ratcheted concentration in the one market with no new entrants. By 1999 the four largest clearing groups held roughly nine-tenths of SME liquidity-management business in England and Wales. What it did to SME credit supply: the customer faced an oligopoly tighter than the cartel era's, minus the cartel's formal price-fixing but with much of its behavioural effect — free-in-credit-looking accounts that paid no interest, opaque money-transmission charges, and switching rates so low that banks could treat the SME base as an annuity. What losses followed here were the customers' rather than the banks': the Cruickshank team would shortly put a number on the excess profits.

docs.title: Cruickshank and the Competition Commission: the complex monopoly, named
docs.where: Module 01 · History & Evolution of UK Business Banking
docs.text: Don Cruickshank's review of UK banking, commissioned by the Treasury in 1998 and published on 20 March 2000, asked whether competition worked for personal customers, for money transmission, and for SMEs. The Cruickshank Report answered no on all three, and was harshest on SME banking: a highly concentrated market, formidable barriers to switching, bank control of the payments plumbing, and persistent excess profits earned from small-business customers. SME banking was referred to the Competition Commission. The Commission's March 2002 report — Competition Commission 2002 — made the finding that titles this module: a complex monopoly under the Fair Trading Act, operated by the largest clearing groups, whose practices restricted price competition in SME banking. The remedies were behavioural rather than structural. As a transitional measure, the big four in England and Wales had, from 2003, to offer SMEs either a current account paying interest at no less than Bank of England base rate minus 2.5 percentage points, or an account free of money-transmission charges, or the choice. Standing undertakings barred bundling — compelling a customer to hold a business current account as the price of a loan or deposit account — with compliance audited for two decades. The afterlife measures the problem's stubbornness. The interest-paying transitional remedy was released in 2007 once judged to have served its purpose; the bundling prohibitions survived until the Competition and Markets Auth

docs.title: When the Money Markets Closed
docs.where: Module 02 · The 2008 Crisis and Its Long Shadow
docs.text: The UK banking crisis did not begin with bad small-business loans. It began with funding. Through the 2000s British banks lent far more than they gathered in deposits, bridging the gap — hundreds of billions of pounds of it — in wholesale markets: securitisation, covered bonds, short-term interbank borrowing. When US sub-prime losses poisoned confidence in bank paper in August 2007, those markets shut. Northern Rock, a mortgage lender with barely any business book, failed within weeks because it could not roll its funding. By October 2008 the problem was solvency: RBS and Lloyds/HBOS took £45.5bn and £20.3bn of taxpayer equity respectively, and every UK bank began a forced march towards more capital, more liquidity and less leverage. For SMEs the transmission was brutal and asymmetric. Small firms do not live on term loans alone; they live on committed and uncommitted overdrafts , invoice finance and property-secured facilities that can be repriced or withdrawn at review. A bank shrinking its balance sheet found the SME book an easy place to deleverage: risk weights were high, collateral values — commercial property above all — were falling, and facilities could be quietly cut at renewal without a front-page headline. Net lending to SMEs turned negative in 2009 and stayed negative into 2013, even with Bank Rate pinned at 0.5% from March 2009. docs.title: Merlin and FLS: The Limits of Exhortation
docs.where: Module 02 · The 2008 Crisis and Its Long Shadow
docs.text: The political response came in two flavours: moral suasion and cheap money. Project Merlin , agreed in February 2011 between the Treasury and the five biggest banks — Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds, RBS and Santander UK — committed the banks to the "capacity and willingness" to make £190bn of gross new lending available to business in 2011, £76bn of it to SMEs. The overall figure was comfortably exceeded. The SME target was missed by roughly £1bn — and the deeper flaw was the metric itself. Merlin counted gross lending, so a bank could hit its number while repayments outran new advances and the net stock of SME credit kept shrinking, which is exactly what happened. There was no penalty mechanism, no clean split between genuinely new money and rolled-over facilities, and no answer to the underlying problem: banks did not want the risk. The Funding for Lending Scheme , launched by the Bank of England and Treasury in mid-2012, attacked the price of funding instead. Banks could swap collateral for Treasury bills at a fee tied to their net lending performance — cheap funding as a reward for growing the book. The first-order effect was real but landed in the wrong place: mortgage pricing fell sharply while SME net lending stayed negative. The April 2013 extension tried to fix the skew, letting banks draw up to £10 of funding for every £1 of net SME lending in 2013; in November 2013 household incentives were removed altogether. docs.title: GRG: What Happened in the Workout Room
docs.where: Module 02 · The 2008 Crisis and Its Long Shadow
docs.text: If one story explains why modern business banking treats its collections and turnaround machinery as a conduct minefield, it is RBS's Global Restructuring Group . GRG was the bank's division for business customers in financial difficulty; roughly 12,000 SMEs passed through it between 2008 and 2013, transferred in as covenants were breached, property revalued or facilities fell due. GRG was also, internally, a profit centre — charging restructuring fees, taking equity stakes, and sitting alongside West Register , an RBS property arm that could end up owning assets sold by the very customers GRG managed. In November 2013 the Tomlinson report — written by Lawrence Tomlinson, then entrepreneur in residence at the business department — alleged that RBS was engineering defaults: manufacturing covenant breaches through revaluations, loading distressed firms with fees, and steering their assets towards West Register. The FCA responded in January 2014 by commissioning a skilled-person review under section 166 of FSMA, conducted by Promontory with Mazars and delivered in September 2016. Promontory did not uphold the most incendiary claim — that RBS deliberately engineered defaults to profit from them — but its findings were damning enough: widespread inappropriate treatment of customers, experienced by most of the sampled firms in some form, with around one in six suffering material financial distress the bank itself caused. docs.title: The Hedges That Strangled
docs.where: Module 02 · The 2008 Crisis and Its Long Shadow
docs.text: Running in parallel was a quieter scandal about products rather than workouts. Through 2001–2011 banks sold interest-rate hedging products — swaps, caps, collars and the baroque "structured collars" — alongside SME loans, frequently as a condition of the lending itself. The pitch was protection against rising rates. When Bank Rate collapsed to 0.5%, the products inverted into a trap: businesses locked into paying fixed against a floating leg near zero, with breakage costs so large that exiting the hedge could cost more than the loan was worth. For a small hotelier or farmer who had wanted a mortgage, not a derivatives position, the cash-flow drain was existential — and, in a grim loop back to the previous section, it was often what pushed a customer into the workout unit. In 2012 the FSA reviewed sales practice, found serious failings, and struck agreements with nine banks to review sales to "non-sophisticated" customers. Just over 20,000 sales were examined; around 14,000 redress offers were accepted; over £2.2bn was paid out, including compensation for consequential losses. The controversial edge was the sophistication test: a cap that excluded customers above certain size thresholds — roughly 10,000 sales — on the theory they should have understood what they bought. docs.title: Children of State Aid: Williams & Glyn and TSB
docs.where: Module 02 · The 2008 Crisis and Its Long Shadow
docs.text: The bailouts came with strings from Brussels. As a condition of approving state aid, the European Commission required RBS to divest a business of 300-plus branches — resurrected under the historic Williams & Glyn brand — and Lloyds to shed the 600-plus branch package known as Project Verde. Both sagas became object lessons in why structural remedies die on IT. RBS agreed a sale to Santander in 2010; Santander walked away in 2012, defeated by the separation. RBS then tried to build Williams & Glyn as a standalone bank for flotation and burned through more than £1.5bn attempting to carve a clone out of its own spaghetti of legacy systems. In 2017, seven years and no divestment later, the Commission accepted the obvious: the sale was abandoned, replaced by an alternative remedies package — £775m, funded by RBS, to promote SME banking competition by other means. That package is the subject of the section after next. Lloyds fared only somewhat better. The Verde sale to the Co-operative Bank collapsed in 2013 when the Co-op's own capital hole surfaced, so Lloyds executed the TSB carve-out instead: launch in September 2013, IPO in June 2014, sale to Spain's Banco Sabadell in 2015 for £1.7bn. Then, in April 2018, TSB ran the most notorious IT migration failure in UK banking history, locking up to 1.9 million customers out of their accounts as it moved off the Lloyds platform; the FCA and PRA eventually fined TSB £48.65m in December 2022 for operational-resilience failings. docs.title: The CMA's 2016 Verdict
docs.where: Module 02 · The 2008 Crisis and Its Long Shadow
docs.text: By 2014 the competition question had outgrown state-aid plumbing, and the Competition and Markets Authority launched a full market investigation into personal current accounts and SME banking. The final report of the CMA 2016 investigation, published on 9 August 2016, was a diagnosis of stagnation rather than abuse: low customer engagement, opaque products, and banks that did not need to compete hard because customers — especially business customers, who overwhelmingly opened accounts with their personal bank and stayed — almost never switched. The CMA deliberately chose behavioural remedies over break-ups. The flagship was the open banking mandate: the nine largest current-account providers were ordered to build a common API standard letting customers share their transaction data with third parties, live from early 2018. Alongside it came mandatory service-quality league tables — banks forced to publish, in branch and in app, independent survey rankings of how likely customers are to recommend them, including business-account rankings — plus overdraft alerts and monthly maximum charges, and transparency tools for SME loan pricing and eligibility. Critics called it timid; no structural change, and switching rates barely moved for years. But the open banking remedy proved to be the sleeper hit of the whole post-crisis settlement: it created the data rails on which fintech SME lenders, cloud accounting integrations and transactional-data lending models were built, and it was co

docs.title: The £775m Consolation Prize
docs.where: Module 02 · The 2008 Crisis and Its Long Shadow
docs.text: The Williams & Glyn failure left RBS owing competition a debt, and the 2017 settlement made it cash. An independent body, Banking Competition Remedies Ltd, was created in 2018 to administer the £775m alternative remedies package: a £425m Capability & Innovation Fund of grants, and £350m for an Incentivised Switching Scheme — £275m of "dowries" paid to challengers for each former Williams & Glyn SME customer they attracted, plus £75m towards customers' switching costs. The grant fund is where today's competitive map was part-drawn. Pool A, awarded February 2019: Metro Bank £120m, Starling £100m, ClearBank £60m in partnership with Tide . Pool B, August 2019: Nationwide £50m, Investec £15m, Co-operative Bank £15m. Pool C handed £10m each to Atom Bank, iwoca, Modulr and Currencycloud; Pool D gave £5m each to fintechs including Codat, Fluidly, Form3, Funding Options and Swoop. The fund then produced its own morality tale: by early 2020 Metro Bank had handed back £50m after admitting it could not deliver its business-banking expansion commitments, and Nationwide returned its entire £50m on abandoning business current accounts altogether. The £100m was recycled into a Pool E and re-granted in 2020–21. docs.title: The Long Shadow at the Impairment Desk
docs.where: Module 02 · The 2008 Crisis and Its Long Shadow
docs.text: Pull the threads together and the crisis bequeathed business banking three permanent conditions. First, a memory of credit famine: SME credit supply is now understood to be procyclical and fragile, which is why every subsequent shock — Brexit, Covid — triggered state guarantee schemes rather than another Merlin-style plea (Module 3 covers what that did to the risk architecture). Second, a conduct settlement written in scar tissue: GRG and IRHP established that how a bank treats a struggling business is a boardroom risk even where the FCA's formal perimeter runs out, and the machinery you work within — segregated support units, fee governance, forbearance oversight, complaint-ready audit trails — is the institutional memory of those scandals. Third, an engineered competitive landscape: state-aid divestments, the CMA's data rails and BCR's cheque-book collectively built the challengers that now discipline incumbent pricing and cherry-pick incumbent customers. For an impairment analyst arriving in BB from retail, the second condition is the one that changes daily work. In cards or mortgages, collections conduct risk is real but industrialised. In BB, every material distressed exposure is a bespoke negotiation with a business owner who has read about GRG — and whose lawyer certainly has. docs.title: Eleven days that built the book
docs.where: Module 03 · COVID, Government Schemes, and the Book That Defines Today
docs.text: When lockdown was announced on 23 March 2020, the Treasury's first answer was the Coronavirus Business Interruption Loan Scheme — a respectable piece of machinery modelled on the old Enterprise Finance Guarantee, with an 80% government guarantee and conventional underwriting left intact. It was also, for the purpose at hand, uselessly slow. Lenders still had to assess viability and affordability; approval queues built while SME cashflow evaporated at the rate of a national economy switching off. Within five weeks the political pressure was unbearable, and on 27 April 2020 the Chancellor announced something genuinely without precedent: the Bounce Back Loan Scheme , designed in days, live on 4 May. The numbers still read like a typo. Across BBLS, CBILS and CLBILS , roughly £79.3bn was approved for about 1.67 million businesses, of which £76.8bn was drawn — £46.5bn of it through BBLS alone, in loans that averaged around £30,000. For context, the entire stock of UK SME bank lending before the pandemic was of the order of £160bn. The state effectively doubled down on the sector in a single year, using the banks as distribution pipes. For you, the consequence is blunt: the modern Business Banking term-lending book is the COVID book, plus whatever has been written around its edges since. docs.title: BBLS anatomy: underwriting, deleted
docs.where: Module 03 · COVID, Government Schemes, and the Book That Defines Today
docs.text: The design brief for BBLS was speed at any cost, and every feature follows from that. Loans of £2,000 to £50,000, capped at 25% of turnover. A 100% government guarantee to the lender — not 80%, not 90%, the lot. A flat 2.5% fixed rate set by the Treasury, identical across every lender and every borrower, which is to say: no pricing for risk whatsoever. A standard six-year term, no fees, no repayments in year one, with the government paying the first twelve months' interest directly to the lender via the Business Interruption Payment. Then the truly radical part. Borrowers applied by self-certification — a short online form attesting to turnover, COVID impact and eligibility. Lenders were explicitly relieved of any obligation to perform credit or affordability checks; their diligence was limited to fraud, anti-money-laundering and KYC screening, mostly automated. Some banks approved and funded loans within hours. Twenty-eight lenders were accredited, but the big incumbents — Barclays among them — wrote the overwhelming majority, because that is where the business current accounts were. It matters that the lender lends its own money. The guarantee is a promise of reimbursement after loss, not funding: the loan sits on the bank's balance sheet, accrues on the bank's books, and defaults into the bank's collections machinery. The state stands behind it, but only if the bank followed the scheme rules — a caveat that turns out to carry real money, as we will see. Impairment Lens A b

docs.where: Module 03 · COVID, Government Schemes, and the Book That Defines Today
docs.text: Self-certified, uncredit-checked lending at 100% guarantee is an open invitation, and everyone involved knew it — the National Audit Office records that ministers consciously accepted a heightened fraud risk as the price of speed. The estimates of how much walked out of the door have moved dramatically. In its October 2020 investigation, the NAO reported working assumptions that 35% to 60% of BBLS lending — £15bn to £26bn — might never come back, combining fraud and credit loss. By March 2021 the department's central estimate was that 37% (£17bn) would not be repaid, of which 11% (£4.9bn) was attributed to fraud. Later departmental accounts revised the fraud figure sharply downward — the 2021–22 BEIS accounts put fraud and error at around £1.1bn, with internal estimates ranging up to £3.5–4.9bn — and the hard number that exists today is lenders' own flagging: as at 31 March 2026, £1.88bn of BBLS drawn value, 4.04% of the book, carries a suspected fraud flag . The fraud itself ranged from the industrial — companies incorporated purely to borrow £50,000 and dissolve — to the mundane inflation of turnover by real businesses to reach the 25% cap. Enforcement runs through the National Investigation Service, the Insolvency Service (director disqualifications, retrospectively pierced dissolutions) and lenders' own recovery teams. docs.title: Pay As You Grow: forbearance by design
docs.where: Module 03 · COVID, Government Schemes, and the Book That Defines Today
docs.text: By early 2021 it was obvious that a large minority of BBLS borrowers could not start repaying on schedule, so the government pre-installed the forbearance. Pay As You Grow gives every BBLS borrower three options, exercisable at will and without lender discretion: extend the term from six years to ten at the same 2.5% rate; switch to interest-only for six months, up to three times over the life of the loan; or take a single six-month full repayment holiday. None of the options affects the guarantee, and none requires evidence of distress. As at March 2026, 37% of BBLS facilities had used at least one PAYG option. Each option does something distinct to arrears emergence. The term extension nearly halves the monthly instalment permanently, converting borrowers who would have defaulted in 2023 into borrowers who may default in 2028 — or may not default at all. The interest-only and holiday options are pure deferral: they push the cash strain a few months to the right and add interest to the tail. Collectively, PAYG flattened and stretched the arrears curve that the scheme's design had guaranteed would arrive, which is why BBLS arrears emerged as a long slow bleed through 2022–2026 rather than a 2022 cliff. docs.where: Module 03 · COVID, Government Schemes, and the Book That Defines Today
docs.text: CBILS deserves to be judged separately, because it is a different animal. An 80% guarantee, facilities up to £5m for businesses with turnover up to £45m, delivered as term loans, overdrafts , invoice finance and asset finance — and, crucially, with underwriting intact. Lenders assessed viability, the government paid the first year's interest and fees, and personal guarantees were barred below £250,000. The £25.8bn CBILS book has behaved accordingly: 64.5% fully repaid by March 2026 against BBLS's 19.4%. CLBILS , for larger corporates (turnover above £45m, facilities eventually up to £200m, dividend restrictions attached), lent £4.5bn and is 96% repaid — for impairment purposes it barely exists. The schemes did not so much end as evolve. The Recovery Loan Scheme launched in April 2021 with an 80% guarantee and a £10m cap; from January 2022 it dropped to 70% and £2m, SMEs only; a third iteration from August 2022 removed the requirement to show COVID impact at all, quietly converting emergency support into a standing SME guarantee programme. In July 2024 it was renamed the Growth Guarantee Scheme : 70% guarantee, up to £2m, full commercial underwriting and pricing, personal guarantees allowed (principal residences excluded). At the June 2025 Spending Review it was extended to March 2030, and by 31 March 2026 it had delivered around £3.6bn through more than seventy lenders. docs.where: Module 03 · COVID, Government Schemes, and the Book That Defines Today
docs.text: All of this runs through the British Business Bank , the state economic-development bank owned by the Department for Business and Trade. The BBB does three things that matter to you. First, accreditation : it vets and admits lenders to each scheme, sets the scheme rules they must follow, and audits compliance. Second, administration : its Scheme Portal is the system of record — every facility, every status change, every claim flows through it, which is why the quarterly gov.uk performance data exists at all. Third, claims : when a guaranteed loan defaults, the lender pursues recovery in line with scheme rules (for BBLS, that means business assets only — personal guarantees were prohibited; for CBILS and successors, normal commercial recovery including any security taken), then submits a guarantee claim through the portal. The guarantor — ultimately the Secretary of State — pays out; recoveries made after settlement are remitted back to government pro rata. The system has teeth. As at March 2026, guarantees had been removed from 14,757 loans worth £1.16bn — roughly £738m following lender discussions (scheme-rule breaches surfaced by audit) and £422m from data errors. Guarantee removal converts a state-backed exposure into an ordinary unsecured SME loan, retrospectively. Impairment Lens Guarantee removal is an LGD cliff, and it is an operational event, not a credit one. docs.title: What a guarantee does to LGD
docs.where: Module 03 · COVID, Government Schemes, and the Book That Defines Today
docs.text: Mechanically, a scheme guarantee enters ECL through loss given default, and it does so with conditions attached. The guaranteed percentage is not a floor gifted at default: the claim must be eligible (the facility originated and serviced within scheme rules), the required pre-claim recovery steps must have been taken, and the cash arrives with a lag — claims are prepared, submitted, reviewed and settled, and discounting that delay is itself a modelled LGD component. On the 80% and 70% schemes, the lender's retained share is pari passu: post-claim recoveries are split with government in guarantee proportion, so the bank cannot recover its 20–30% strip first. Then there is the accounting question your desk will meet constantly: is the guarantee integral to the loan's contractual terms — in which case its expected cash flows sit inside the ECL calculation and directly suppress LGD — or is it a separate financial guarantee contract, recognised as a distinct reimbursement asset with the loan provisioned gross? For the COVID schemes, where the guarantee was part of the lending proposition from inception, the integral guarantee treatment is the standard answer, but the distinction, its edge cases and its disclosure consequences get full treatment in Module 7. For now, hold the flag. Impairment Lens This is why guaranteed-versus-unguaranteed is the first cut of every BB ECL pack. docs.title: Run-off: the book in 2025–2026
docs.where: Module 03 · COVID, Government Schemes, and the Book That Defines Today
docs.text: The COVID book was originated in 2020–21 on six-year terms, so the contractual maturity wall sits in 2026–27 — with the PAYG -extended tail stretching to 2030–31. The March 2026 scheme data shows what run-off looks like from the guarantor's side. Of BBLS facilities: 19.4% fully repaid, 46.9% on schedule, 3.9% in arrears, 0.7% defaulted awaiting claim — and 28.3% already settled under the guarantee. Across all three schemes, settled claims total £12.98bn, £11.8bn of it BBLS. Set against the NAO's early loss assumptions of £15–26bn, the outturn is bad but at the benign end of what was feared; against any normal lending standard, a book where more than a quarter of facilities have been claimed is extraordinary. Two dynamics define the residual. First, adverse selection by survivorship: the strong borrowers prepaid or amortised out years ago, so arrears and default rates measured on the remaining book rise mechanically each quarter even if no individual borrower deteriorates. Second, composition: what is left is disproportionately PAYG-extended, thin-file, and — where guarantees have been removed or claims rejected — unguaranteed. The write-off line, meanwhile, needs reading with care: fraud write-offs (claimed, state-funded, criminally pursued) and credit write-offs (ordinary failures of ordinary businesses) run through different processes at different speeds. docs.title: Where Business Banking Lives
docs.text: Start with the corporate architecture, because at Barclays the org chart is also the regulatory perimeter. Since January 2019 the group has run two principal banks: Barclays Bank UK PLC — the ring-fenced bank, branded Barclays UK — and Barclays Bank PLC, the non-ring-fenced entity that houses the investment bank and international business. Ring-fencing , the post-crisis regime born of the Vickers Commission, forces UK retail and small-business deposits into a legally separate, separately capitalised entity. Business Banking sits squarely inside the fence. The reporting map was redrawn in February 2024, when the group's investor update carved Barclays into five divisions: Barclays UK, the UK Corporate Bank , the Private Bank & Wealth Management, the Investment Bank, and the US Consumer Bank. Within the Barclays UK division, segment reporting splits income three ways: Personal Banking, Barclaycard Consumer UK, and Business Banking. That third line is your world. The boundary that matters most to an impairment analyst is the handoff at the top: clients with annual turnover above roughly £6.5m belong to the UK Corporate Bank, a separate division with its own coverage teams, its own credit appetite and — critically — its own impairment disclosure. Everything below that line, from the sole trader with a card reader to the £6m-turnover wholesaler, is Business Banking. docs.text: Barclays banks roughly one million SME clients — a figure the bank itself cites when marketing its Business Prosperity Index, which claims proprietary sight of about a million small businesses and a quarter of all UK corporates (as at 2025). That client count makes Barclays one of the big-four incumbents in business current accounts, alongside Lloyds, NatWest and HSBC. Now look at the balance sheet, because the asymmetry is the whole story. At end-2025, Business Banking loans stood at £17.9bn, down from £19.7bn a year earlier — the decline driven, in the bank's own words, by continued repayment of government scheme lending. Deposits: £51.9bn (2024: £52.8bn). Read that again. The segment holds nearly three pounds of deposits for every pound it lends. Business Banking income was £2,126m in FY25, up 6% on FY24's £2,004m, and up from £1,905m in FY23 — growth powered overwhelmingly by deposit margin in a higher-rate world, not by lending expansion. For context, the whole Barclays UK division carried £215.6bn of customer loans and £244.7bn of deposits at end-2025, and delivered a return on tangible equity of 20.7%. Barclays has pledged headline lending support — £22bn made available for Business Banking and UK Corporate Banking clients in 2025 — but pledges are capacity, not stock. The stock keeps shrinking as BBLS balances amortise away faster than new lending replaces them. docs.title: The Current Account Is the Product
docs.text: Strip Business Banking to its economics and it is a deposit franchise with lending attached. The anchor product is the business current account : Barclays holds one of the largest BCA books in the UK, and everything else — overdrafts, term loans, card acquiring, FX — hangs off that primary relationship. In the post-2016 CMA world where switching is subsidised and challengers are given away accounts for free, the incumbents' moat is inertia plus breadth: the ability to serve a client from first invoice to £6.5m turnover without changing bank. The lending shelf is deliberately simple. Unsecured business loans and overdrafts for working capital; secured term lending and commercial mortgages for the larger end; participation in the British Business Bank's Growth Guarantee Scheme for marginal credits; and referral or partnership routes for specialist needs like asset and invoice finance rather than deep in-house manufacturing. Barclays' underwriting edge, such as it is, comes from transactional data: it can see a decade of a client's cash flows through the BCA and the acquiring rails before it advances a pound. What Barclays does not do is chase the aggressive end of SME credit. The FY25 numbers show a bank content to let the government-scheme legacy run off, keep new origination disciplined, and earn its return on the liability side. docs.title: Barclaycard Payments and the Brookfield Turn
docs.text: The genuinely differentiating asset in the Barclays SME proposition has long been Barclaycard Payments — the merchant acquiring business that puts Barclays on both sides of the till. Industry analyses rank it among the top two UK acquirers, processing on the order of 8.7 billion transactions a year (approximate, as at 2025). No neobank competitor owns an acquirer of that scale; for Barclays it meant a second data feed on client health — you see the revenue arriving, not just the balance sitting. Then came April 2025. Barclays announced a strategic partnership with Brookfield Asset Management for the UK merchant acquiring business: Barclays injects around £400m over three years to modernise the platform, Brookfield takes on operational transformation, and — the structural punchline — Brookfield holds the option to acquire roughly 70–80% of the business between years three and seven. Read plainly: Barclays is preparing to majority-exit merchant acquiring while retaining a minority stake and the client relationship. Strategically this mirrors what most European banks concluded a decade earlier — acquiring is a scale-and-technology game better played by specialists (Worldpay, Adyen, Teya) than by bank cost centres. But it dilutes a differentiator. docs.text: Eagle Labs is the strategy asset that never touches the credit book. Launched in 2015 as repurposed branch space for start-up incubation, it grew into a national network of sites and programmes for tech entrepreneurs — mentoring, ecosystem partnerships, sector programmes from healthtech in Scotland to cyber in the South West. Its establishment credibility peaked when the government chose it, controversially over Tech Nation, to deliver the Digital Growth Grant : £12.09m of public funding from April 2023 to March 2025, targeting support for more than 22,000 businesses with at least 80% outside London. Why should an impairment analyst care about an incubator? Because Eagle Labs is the top of a funnel. Start-ups incubated today are BCA clients tomorrow and borrowers the year after; the franchise logic is origination at the point of company formation. It also buys Barclays something harder to price — presence in the high-growth segment where challengers like Starling and Tide otherwise dominate the narrative. The same logic drives the digital stack. docs.title: The Book from the Impairment Seat
docs.text: Sit in the Barclays BB impairment chair in 2026 and the book in front of you has three strata. First, the BBLS legacy: Barclays was one of the largest Bounce Back lenders, and although balances have amortised hard — the run-off is precisely why segment loans fell from £19.7bn to £17.9bn during 2025 — a material tail remains, much of it stretched to ten-year terms under Pay As You Grow . These loans carry a 100% government guarantee treated as an integral guarantee : expected recoveries from the state flow into LGD, so even a defaulted Bounce Back loan generates almost no ECL for the bank. The credit risk never left; it was assigned to the taxpayer at origination. Second, the secured book — commercial mortgages and charged-asset term lending at the larger end — where property collateral does the LGD work and losses concentrate in workout timing rather than severity. Third, the clean unsecured book: overdrafts and term loans priced off transactional data, which is where genuine loss content lives and where staging judgement earns its keep. The sector tilt is the UK SME economy itself — services-heavy, with the familiar stress concentrations in hospitality, retail and construction that every insolvency cycle revisits. And the structural trend an analyst must internalise: as the guaranteed stratum runs off, the surviving book's average risk profile rises mechanically. docs.title: A Concentrated Front, a Dispersed War
docs.text: Seen from the account ledger, UK business banking is a settled oligopoly. The four largest groups — Lloyds, NatWest, HSBC and Barclays — still hold roughly 85 per cent of business current accounts , a concentration that has survived two decades of regulatory engineering designed to break it. Seen from the credit ledger, the picture inverts. In 2025, challenger and specialist banks wrote 60 per cent of the £68 billion of gross bank lending to SMEs — the fourth consecutive year they out-lent the big five, and the highest share the British Business Bank has ever recorded. Accounts are concentrated; credit is dispersed. That inversion is the most important structural fact in this module, and it is not an accident of marketing. It is the residue of incumbent choices. After 2008, and again after the pandemic, the large banks pulled capital, branch staff and appetite out of the middle of the SME risk curve. What they kept was the franchise: the payments float, the safest secured lending, the seasoned back book. What they released — asset finance on eight-year-old trucks, bridging on secondary property, unsecured working capital for cafés — was picked up by lenders built for exactly those niches. Nearly every competitor on this map exists because an incumbent decided some risk was not worth holding. For an impairment analyst the map earns its keep three ways. docs.title: The Incumbents: Retreat in Good Order
docs.text: Lloyds Banking Group runs the largest SME franchise in the country, trading as Lloyds in England and Wales and Bank of Scotland north of the border. Its advantage is brutal and simple: the biggest retail deposit base in the UK, which makes its marginal cost of funds lower than anyone else's. That cheap float funds a conservative book — secured, seasoned, relationship-managed at the top end, increasingly automated below it. Lloyds is not where SME credit innovation happens; it is where SME credit margin goes to be harvested, and where the run-off of Covid-era balances has been managed with the patience only cheap funding buys. NatWest carries the historic number-one position in SME market share — the inheritance of the old RBS, which was for decades the default business bank of Britain. The inheritance cuts both ways. The GRG affair taught the group, expensively, that the treatment of distressed SMEs is a conduct exposure as much as a credit one, and its workout posture has been visibly more careful since. Its answer to the challengers was to build its own: Mettle , a standalone app-based business account, and Tyl , a merchant-acquiring service that has grown fast enough to justify a 2026 technology partnership with Endava. Both are competent; neither has changed the race. HSBC UK courts the internationally minded SME — trade finance, multi-currency, supply chains — and serves the smaller end through Kinetic , its app-based small-business platform. docs.text: The account-side challengers are, to a striking degree, a state-funded insurgency. The BCR pot — £775 million of RBS state-aid remedy money — and the incentivised switching scheme paid fintechs to take customers the CMA's earlier remedies had failed to move. It worked, up to a point: the challengers won accounts. What they have mostly not won is the loan book. Starling is the flagship: around 9.7 per cent of the SME business-account market on its own reporting, revenue of £714 million in FY2025, deposit-rich and conspicuously lending-light. Its instructive scar is the BBLS book. Having lent at pandemic speed under a 100 per cent guarantee, Starling identified loans whose origination checks had not met scheme conditions, volunteered to strip the government guarantee from them, and booked a £28.2 million provision in FY2025 — on top of a £29 million FCA fine for financial-crime control failures. The lesson is precise: a guarantee is a conditional contract, not a property of the loan. Its credit is largely originated through partners. docs.title: Marketplaces, Embedded Credit and the Payments Flank
docs.text: Funding Circle pioneered marketplace lending in the UK: originate the loan, sell it to institutional investors, keep the servicing fee, hold none of the risk. Then reality edited the model. The US business was sold, and the growth engine became FlexiPay — a working-capital line held on Funding Circle's own balance sheet. docs.title: What the Field Teaches the Impairment Desk
docs.text: Pull the threads together and five working rules emerge. First, competition is a credit-quality force, not a commercial nuisance: every account or asset a rival skims changes the composition of what remains, and adverse selection arrives in the flow long before it shows in the arrears. Second, the loss-experience range across this map — 4.5 basis points at OakNorth against double-digit fraud losses on BBLS — is not a spread of asset classes; it is a spread of underwriting designs, which means it is controllable and comparable. Third, guarantee integrity is an origination property: Starling's provision is what it costs when the paperwork behind a guarantee claim fails. Fourth, growth flatters: any book compounding at 20 per cent has an observed default rate that understates its destination. Fifth, and least visible: funding models decide behaviour under stress. BCA-float incumbents can afford patience; savings-funded specialists can hold but reprice; wholesale-funded lenders retrench the moment facilities tighten. When the marginal lenders withdraw, the weak borrower's refinancing options vanish exactly when needed — cure rates fall, workout recoveries thin, and Stage 3 outcomes deteriorate across the market, including on the book of a bank that never changed its own appetite. Barclays sits in the middle of this field as a full-service incumbent with a payments franchise the insurgents envy and a risk curve the specialists keep shortening from below. docs.title: Why SME PD refuses to behave like retail PD
docs.text: Your retail career was built on a luxury so pervasive you probably stopped noticing it: homogeneity. A credit card book is millions of near-identical exposures, scored on near-identical data, defaulting in statistically well-behaved numbers every single month. The law of large numbers does most of the work; your models refine the residual. An SME book grants you none of this. A dental practice, a scaffolding subcontractor, a SaaS startup burning venture money and a fourth-generation sheep farmer can all sit in the same portfolio segment, sharing almost nothing except a business current account at the same bank. Banks have historically dealt with this heterogeneity through three distinct lending technologies. Financial-statement lending underwrites the accounts: ratios, gearing, interest cover, debtor quality. It works for larger SMEs with audited numbers and falls apart below that, for reasons the next section makes painful. Relationship lending underwrites the person: a relationship manager accumulates soft information — the state of the yard, the succession plan, whether the founder's optimism is earned — that never appears in any dataset. It is expensive, unscalable, and was systematically stripped out of UK banking as branch networks and local credit discretion were centralised. docs.title: Companies House: a public ledger with holes in it
docs.text: Retail underwriting spoiled you with the bureau: deep, standardised, refreshed monthly, covering essentially every adult you would ever lend to. The BB equivalent is Companies House — free, public, statutory, and riddled with exemptions. Since April 2025 a company qualifies as "small" with turnover up to £15m, a balance sheet up to £7.5m and up to 50 employees — thresholds raised roughly 50% in one move, reclassifying an estimated 133,000 entities downward. Small companies need no audit, and can file filleted accounts : a balance sheet, some notes, and — critically — no profit and loss account. Micro-entities file even less under FRS 105. The overwhelming majority of your borrowers, in other words, are legally entitled to show the public register a snapshot of what they own while concealing whether they make any money. Then there is the lag. A private company has nine months from its year end to file. Accounts made up to December 2025 can arrive in September 2026 — and remain the freshest public financials until late 2027. On the day you read them, the numbers can be nearly two years stale. Reform is perpetually imminent: the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 promised to abolish the filleted option and force small companies to file a P&L, but those reforms were paused in early 2026, and mandatory software-only filing has slipped to April 2028. What did land, in November 2025, was mandatory identity verification for directors and people with significant co

docs.title: Sectors, SIC codes and concentration you never had in retail
docs.text: Every UK company self-declares a SIC code at incorporation — a five-digit label chosen from a drop-down, frequently wrong, rarely updated as the business pivots. On this shaky foundation banks build sector segmentation, concentration limits, pricing differentials and the mapping of macroeconomic scenarios to portfolios. Treat SIC data the way you learned to treat self-declared income on a 2006 mortgage application: useful, directional, and not to be confused with truth. Sector matters in BB in a way it simply does not in retail, because SME failure is brutally cyclical and sector-concentrated. Construction is the perennial leader: roughly 17% of all company insolvencies, with around 3,800 construction firms entering insolvency in the twelve months to March 2026 — down about 7% on the prior year but still nearly a fifth above pre-pandemic levels. The mechanics are structural: fixed-price contracts signed before costs move, long subcontractor chains where one main-contractor failure cascades downward, retentions withheld, margins of 2–3% with no buffer. Hospitality runs on thin margins, seasonal cash flow, energy costs and discretionary consumer spending; retail adds structural decline to the same cocktail. When you read that overall insolvencies in England and Wales are running at around 2,000–2,100 a month through 2025–26, remember those failures are not spread evenly — they pool in these sectors. docs.title: The working-capital cycle, read through a current account
docs.text: The working-capital cycle is the elapsed time between a business paying cash out and getting cash back: stock days plus debtor days minus creditor days. It is the single most useful lens for reading an SME, because most SME deaths are cash-flow deaths — profitable-on-paper businesses that ran out of money waiting to be paid. A subcontractor buys materials and pays wages weekly, invoices monthly, waits 60–90 days for payment and has 5% retained for a year: an enormous positive cycle, permanently hungry for funding. A pub takes cash tonight and pays its brewery on 30-day terms: a negative cycle, generating float. Same turnover, opposite credit needs — the builder needs an overdraft or invoice finance ; the pub needs almost nothing until the day trade stops. Now put yourself in the bank's seat, watching the BCA . Credit turnover — the sum of money flowing in — is a live proxy for sales receipts. Its trend, its seasonality, its volatility, its concentration (one big customer or many small ones) are all legible from the account alone. So is distress, and earlier than any other source: turnover drifting down quarter on quarter; an overdraft that stops swinging back into credit and hardens into permanent debt; direct debits bouncing, then being cancelled; the tell-tale rhythm of HMRC payments stretching from monthly to sporadic; round-sum transfers out to directors' personal accounts as confidence fails. docs.title: Behavioural scoring: the account never lies for long
docs.text: Behavioural scoring in BB is the industrialisation of the bank manager's glance at the ledger. Monthly (or faster), a model consumes the account's vital signs — credit turnover trend, balance volatility, days in excess of limit, unpaid items, credit-to-debit ratios, time since last cleared balance — and produces a score that outperforms any financial-statement model for the simple reason that it is current . The accounts are a photograph from last year; the behavioural score is a pulse. Conceptually this is the same technology you ran on cards. The differences are in the plumbing and the stakes. The features are business-shaped: VAT-quarter seasonality has to be modelled or it generates false alarms; a single large customer paying late can crater a month's turnover without meaning anything. Score deterioration drives real interventions — limit reductions, facility reviews, watchlist entry, transfer toward the business support unit — not just contact strategies. Impairment Lens Here is the load-bearing fact for your day job: in BB collective books, behavioural score deterioration is typically the primary SICR trigger. A score migration breaches the relative-PD threshold, the exposure moves to Stage 2 , and the provision flips from 12-month to lifetime ECL — on an SME that has missed no payment and breached no covenant. Because SME lifetime PDs are far higher than retail-mortgage ones, the coverage step-up is violent: tens of basis points to several percent in one staging move.

docs.title: Open banking: reading someone else's current account
docs.text: Everything in the last two sections rested on a monopoly: only the account-holding bank could see the BCA. Open banking broke that. Since the CMA forced the nine largest current-account providers to open API access in 2018, any authorised lender can — with the customer's consent — pull months of transaction history at the point of application. Adoption stopped being niche some time ago: the UK passed 15 million open banking users in mid-2026, with connections approaching 19 million. The challengers built their underwriting on it. iwoca was among the first SME lenders to plumb open banking directly into credit decisions, reading live turnover instead of stale accounts, and has kept scaling — closing a £250m funding facility in July 2026 to expand UK SME lending, with mid-sized loans of £50,000–£100,000 jumping to 42% of its applications in early 2026. Tide sees its members' transaction flows natively, as do Starling and the other app-based business banks; Funding Circle and the broader fintech lending cohort consume the same feeds through APIs. The Data Use and Access Act now points beyond payments data toward open finance — SME lending data included — which will widen the pipe further. Read the strategic consequence carefully: the incumbent's century-old informational moat — being the only one who could see the account — is being commoditised, one consent screen at a time. What remains defensible is the interpretive layer: models, sector knowledge, workout capability. Data ad

docs.title: Security, the waterfall, and where LGD is actually decided
docs.text: Retail LGD was a property valuation, a haircut and a repossession timeline. BB security is a zoo, and the differences decide your recoveries. The classic bank instrument is the debenture : a single document taking fixed and floating charges over everything the company owns. A fixed charge attaches to specific, identifiable assets — the freehold, plant, sometimes the book debts if control is real — and the company cannot deal with them without consent. A floating charge hovers over the circulating assets — stock, debtors, work in progress — letting the business trade them freely until insolvency crystallises the charge over whatever happens to remain. That phrase should trouble you: whatever remains , at the exact moment a failing business has run down stock, stretched collections and burned cash, is reliably less than the covenant schedule imagined. Then the priority waterfall takes its cuts. Fixed-charge holders are paid from their asset first. From floating-charge realisations, the order runs: insolvency practitioners' fees and expenses; ordinary preferential creditors (chiefly employees); then — since December 2020 — HMRC as secondary preferential creditor for VAT, PAYE, employee NICs and CIS deductions, with no cap on age or amount. Since failing SMEs almost universally stretch HMRC before anyone else, this claim is routinely large. docs.title: Same Standard, Different Animal
docs.text: Nothing in the standard changes when you cross the corridor from retail to Business Banking. IFRS 9 is the same text; ECL is still the probability-weighted present value of cash shortfalls; the engine still multiplies PD , LGD and EAD and discounts at the effective interest rate. What changes is the terrain the standard has to be applied to — and the terrain changes almost everything about how the number is actually produced. Five shifts matter. First, data density collapses as exposure size rises: a card book gives you millions of homogeneous accounts refreshed monthly by the bureau; an SME book gives you a fat tail of micro-businesses that behave almost like retail and a thin head of larger relationships where defaults are rare and every case is idiosyncratic. Second, qualitative human judgment — relationship-manager gradings, watchlist committees — stops being colour and becomes a model input with a direct P&L consequence. Third, staging migrates in lumps rather than smooth score-driven flows, because the triggers are events, not deltas. Fourth, government guarantees from the Covid schemes sit inside the loss estimate itself, producing books that are visibly stressed and almost unprovisioned at the same time. Fifth, the share of the final number that comes from management judgment — individual assessments, PMAs , scenario choices — is far higher than anything you will have signed off in mortgages. The rest of this module takes those shifts one at a time. Keep one quest

docs.title: Staging When the Data Runs Thin
docs.text: In retail, SICR is an industrialised, quantitative affair: residual lifetime PD compared against origination, bureau score deltas, arrears buckets rolling forward month by month, and the 30-days-past-due backstop sweeping up whatever the models miss. The signals are dense, continuous and cheap. Business Banking keeps the same Stage 1 → Stage 2 architecture but has to feed it differently, because above the micro end the behavioural data that powers retail SICR simply is not there in usable volume. At the smallest end — sole traders, one-director companies — the business current account is actually a rich behavioural asset, and transactional-data triggers do real work: a sustained collapse in BCA credit turnover of, say, a third against the prior year is one of the most reliable early-warning signals a bank holds, often firing months before any missed payment. But as exposures grow, staging leans increasingly on discrete, qualitative events. The canonical BB SICR triggers are: entry onto the watchlist ; a covenant breach on an interest-cover, leverage or loan-to-value test — a trigger with no retail equivalent at all; BCA turnover collapse; sector flags applied at SIC-code level when a committee downgrades commercial real estate, construction or hospitality; hardcore overdraft utilisation and repeated excess requests; and late or qualified accounts at Companies House. The 30 DPD backstop still applies — but treat it as a smoke alarm in a house already burning. A struggling firm

docs.title: Collective by Default, Individual by Exception
docs.text: The mass of the SME book is provisioned exactly as you would expect: collective assessment , with exposures pooled by product, size band, sector and grade, and modelled PD, LGD and EAD applied across each pool. That works for the same reason it works in cards — the accounts are numerous, individually small, and statistically well-behaved in aggregate. It stops working at the top of the book. Every bank sets thresholds — commonly a gross exposure in the low single-digit millions, though the level is house policy, not regulation — above which a Stage 3 case, and often a watchlist Stage 2 case, flips out of the models entirely and becomes individually assessed . Size is not the only trigger: fraud, litigation, complex or cross-collateralised security, or an active insolvency process will push a smaller case into individual treatment because modelled parameters have nothing sensible to say about it. The individual assessment itself is a DCF workout . The case manager — usually in the business support unit — constructs the realistic recovery strategies: trade-out under a restructured facility, consensual sale of the business or assets, or enforcement through administration or liquidation. Each strategy gets its own cash-flow projection — asset realisations net of costs and prior charges, guarantee recoveries, contributions under personal guarantees, time to realise — discounted at the original effective interest rate.
