docs.title: The Guarantee Question: Integral or Not
docs.text: The Covid schemes left BB books carrying something retail never had to think about: a government guarantee wired into the loss estimate. BBLS came with a 100% guarantee of principal and interest; CBILS and its successors with 80% (70% under the current Growth Guarantee Scheme). The accounting question is where that guarantee lives — and it is one of the genuinely contested corners of IFRS 9. IFRS 9 says ECL cash flows include cash from credit enhancements that are integral to the contractual terms of the loan and not separately recognised. If the guarantee qualifies, expected claims sit inside the ECL calculation as a recovery — mechanically, a reduction in LGD. If it does not qualify, the bank must measure ECL gross and recognise the expected reimbursement as a separate asset, IAS 37-style — same net balance sheet, very different presentation, coverage ratios and audit trail. The standard never defines integral , and the IFRS Interpretations Committee's staff analysis left it as a judgment on facts and circumstances. UK banks converged on the answer that the scheme guarantees are integral : the guarantee exists only because the loan was written under scheme rules, was in place at origination, is held by the lender under the British Business Bank's agreement, and was not purchased separately. The consequence is one of the strangest sights in UK bank reporting. Staging reflects the borrower's credit risk, not the expected loss — so a deteriorated BBLS loan sits in Stage 2 or S

docs.title: PMAs: The Judgment Layer
docs.text: Every ECL estimate carries adjustments, but BB carries proportionally more of them. A post-model adjustment — or overlay , the terms blur, though some houses reserve overlay for economics-level adjustments and PMA for model-deficiency fixes — is a quantified amendment to modelled ECL for a risk the models cannot see. The reasons BB accumulates them follow directly from everything above: the models are coarser and rebuilt less often than retail's; default data is thin, so calibration uncertainty is real; sector event risk — a CRE repricing, an energy-cost shock to hospitality, reservoir-level rules hitting agriculture — arrives faster than any model redevelopment cycle; insolvency responds to stress with a lag no GDP-conditioned model captures cleanly; and the guarantee books carry claim-eligibility risk that has no modelled home at all. Typical BB PMAs in current disclosures: sector overlays on CRE, construction and hospitality; affordability and refinance-risk adjustments for borrowers rolling off cheap fixed-rate debt; adjustments for the lag between economic stress and insolvency outcomes; and guarantee-recovery haircuts. The PRA has made the completeness and governance of PMAs a running theme of its Dear CFO letters — the September 2025 letter again flagged elevated model risk amid macro and geopolitical uncertainty, pressed firms to challenge whether PMAs capture risks their models were never built for, and repeated the expectation that persistent overlays be folded back

docs.title: The Low Default Portfolio Problem
docs.text: Move up the size scale and you hit a statistical wall retail never faces: the low default portfolio . A grade in a mid-corporate or larger-SME rating scale might see a handful of defaults a year — sometimes none. You cannot estimate a stable PD from that; the confidence interval around the estimate is wider than the estimate itself. The responses are familiar from IRB practice and carry straight into IFRS 9. Rating comes from expert-judgment scorecards blending financials, sector and management assessment rather than pure statistical models. Calibration borrows from outside — external benchmarks, rating-agency corporate default studies, national insolvency rates — and an explicit margin of conservatism is added to acknowledge estimation uncertainty. For specialised lending such as CRE development, banks use slotting-like approaches: exposures mapped to a small number of supervisory-style categories, each carrying an assigned risk band, in place of a modelled PD altogether. For ECL specifically, the pain point is converting these through-the-cycle-flavoured grades into the point-in-time, forward-looking term structures IFRS 9 demands. The usual machinery — macro scalars applied to a master scale — preserves rank-ordering well but leaves the level of lifetime PD genuinely uncertain, and grade-level backtesting is close to impossible when annual defaults per grade are countable on one hand. docs.title: Forward-Looking Economics for Firms, Not Households
docs.text: Retail forward-looking economics runs on a famous pairing: unemployment drives PD, HPI drives secured LGD. Neither does much work for an SME book. The variables that actually move SME ECL are GDP growth (demand for the borrower's product), the corporate insolvency rate (the closest thing to a direct default-rate anchor), Bank of England base rate (most BB lending floats over base, so rate rises transmit straight into debt service — the opposite of a fixed-rate mortgage book), and commercial real estate indices (collateral values behind commercial mortgages and much secured trading-business lending). Sector-level output indices matter too, because SME stress is rarely uniform: in the twelve months to December 2025, construction, wholesale/retail and hospitality alone accounted for roughly 47% of the c.23,900 UK company insolvencies, with the overall insolvency rate at about 53 per 10,000 active companies. Designing the multiple economic scenarios for an SME book differs accordingly. The insolvency-rate path does the heavy lifting, and it behaves badly: insolvencies lag GDP, then spike late-cycle and non-linearly — the post-Covid years proved the point, when government support suppressed insolvencies through 2020–21 before they surged past pre-pandemic levels from 2022 onwards even as GDP recovered. A model conditioned on GDP alone missed that entirely, which is precisely why insolvency-lag PMAs exist. Downside scenarios and their weights therefore matter more than in retail: t

docs.title: The road in: how a loan becomes a case
docs.text: In retail, default arrives as data: a missed direct debit, a bucket roll, a dialler strategy. In business banking it arrives as a story, and usually a slow one. A £750k exposure to a haulage firm does not roll from bucket one to bucket three; it sends signals for months — hardcore utilisation of the overdraft , returned payments, requests for temporary excesses, a covenant breach quietly waived, an HMRC time-to-pay arrangement the relationship manager hears about second-hand. Arrears on the term loan are often the last signal, not the first, because businesses starve every other creditor before they starve the bank that holds a debenture over everything and a personal guarantee over the director's house. The machinery that responds is layered. Early deterioration puts the name on the watchlist — heightened monitoring, still front-line owned. Sustained deterioration triggers the transfer decision: the case moves out of the relationship team and into the bank's Business Support function, where a specialist decides whether this is a viable business with a fixable problem or a dead business with a recoverable balance sheet. Everything downstream — regime choice, recovery path, provision, write-off — flows from that fork. This module walks the whole chain, because a Stage 3 provision on a BB exposure is not a formula; it is a forecast of which door the company will exit through, and each door has its own price.

docs.title: Business Support, and the long shadow of GRG
docs.text: Every large UK bank runs a turnaround unit — Barclays' Business Support, and its peers' equivalents — that takes deteriorating SME and mid-market cases and works them: restructured facilities, extended terms, capital repayment holidays, sometimes an insisted-upon independent business review by an accountancy firm. The unit's stated objective is return-to-health; its structural reality is that it also protects the bank's position, and the tension between those two jobs is the most conduct-scarred territory in UK banking. The scar is GRG . RBS's Global Restructuring Group took in some 12,000 struggling SMEs after 2008; Lawrence Tomlinson's 2013 report alleged businesses were being engineered into default and stripped. The FCA commissioned a skilled-person review under section 166 of FSMA — Promontory reported in 2016 — which found widespread inappropriate treatment of customers and judged some of it systematic, rooted in RBS's failure to manage the conflict between GRG's turnaround and commercial objectives. The FCA ultimately took no enforcement action, for a reason every BB analyst should internalise: commercial lending is largely unregulated activity, so the conduct perimeter that protects a mortgage customer simply did not apply. The industry response was structural rather than statutory — rebuilt turnaround units with fair-treatment frameworks, separation of turnaround advice from recovery profit incentives, independent case oversight, and board-level appetite statements a

docs.title: Liquidation: the CVL machine and its compulsory cousin
docs.text: Most UK corporate insolvencies are not dramatic restructurings; they are burials. A creditors' voluntary liquidation is a director-initiated wind-up: the board concedes insolvency, shareholders resolve to liquidate, and an insolvency practitioner is appointed — the whole entry process can complete in two to three weeks. The company stops trading, assets are sold at break-up values, and the liquidator distributes according to the statutory waterfall. CVL is the exit route for the small, asset-light SME — the café, the subcontractor, the ten-person agency — and it dominates the statistics precisely because that is what most failing companies are. For a lender the arithmetic is bleak: fixed charge realisations (property, book debts under a properly structured charge) can recover well, but floating-charge and unsecured recoveries are typically low single-digit pence in the pound and very often nil. First distributions may arrive within a year; final ones commonly take one to two, sometimes longer where litigation or antecedent-transaction claims run. Compulsory liquidation is the same destination reached hostile: a creditor — very frequently HMRC — petitions the court to wind the company up. It is slower (months from petition to order), the Official Receiver or an appointed liquidator inherits a business that has usually been dying untreated for longer, and recoveries are correspondingly worse. docs.title: Administration and the pre-pack
docs.text: Administration is the regime with ambition. An administrator takes control under a statutory purpose hierarchy — rescue the company as a going concern; failing that, achieve a better result for creditors than immediate winding-up; failing that, realise property for secured and preferential creditors — and the company gets a moratorium on creditor enforcement while they work. Crucially for banks, a lender holding a qualifying floating charge under its debenture can appoint an administrator out of court, quickly, which is why the debenture is as much a control document as a security document. Administration lasts twelve months, extendable; trading administrations that sell the business as a going concern can return materially more than break-up — this is where secured recoveries of 50–80p on well-collateralised exposures live — while failed administrations converge on liquidation outcomes. Expect a one-to-two-year path from appointment to final distribution. The pre-pack is administration compressed to a single morning: the sale of the business is negotiated before appointment and executed immediately after, preserving goodwill, contracts and jobs before the insolvency stigma destroys them. It maximises value and minimises transparency in the same motion — especially when the buyer is the old management. Since 30 April 2021, a substantial disposal to a connected person within the first eight weeks requires either creditor approval or an independent evaluator 's written opinion

docs.title: The compromise tools: CVA, Part 26A, and the moratorium
docs.text: Three regimes try to fix the company without killing it. The company voluntary arrangement is a deal with unsecured creditors — approved by 75% by value of those voting — under which the company trades on and pays contributions, typically over three to five years, with landlords and trade creditors compromised and secured creditors untouched without consent. CVAs had their cultural moment in casual dining and retail circa 2018–20; they are now rare (186 in the whole of 2025) and their track record is poor — historically roughly half fail into a subsequent insolvency, which means a lender should treat a CVA less as a recovery outcome than as a slower route to one. The Part 26A restructuring plan , introduced by CIGA 2020, is the heavyweight tool: a court-sanctioned compromise that can bind secured creditors and — via cross-class cram-down — impose the deal on entire dissenting classes, provided no one is worse off than in the relevant alternative. It is powerful and expensive: two court hearings, valuation fights, seven-figure adviser costs. Only a dozen plans had been registered by late 2022, and while mid-market usage has grown since, it remains an exceptional event in a BB book — you will see one when a leveraged, multi-banked borrower restructures, and your exposure may be crammed down whether Barclays votes for it or not. The standalone moratorium , also from CIGA 2020, gives a distressed company an initial 20 business days of breathing space (extendable to 40, further wi

docs.title: The waterfall: HMRC's return and the prescribed part
docs.text: Every recovery number in this module resolves to a queue. Fixed-charge realisations go to the fixed-charge holder, net of costs. Then, from floating-charge assets: the insolvency's expenses; ordinary preferential creditors (chiefly employee wage and pension claims); then — restored on 1 December 2020 by the Finance Act 2020 — HMRC as secondary preferential creditor for taxes the company collected on the Crown's behalf: VAT, PAYE, employee NICs and CIS deductions. Corporation tax stays unsecured. The restoration is uncapped and has no age limit on the tax debt, and its effect is mechanical: in a VAT-heavy or labour-heavy business that has been surviving on unremitted tax — which is exactly what distressed SMEs do — HMRC's claim can consume the entire floating-charge pot before the bank sees a penny. Behind HMRC sits the prescribed part : a statutory carve-out from floating-charge realisations for unsecured creditors — 50% of the first £10,000 of net property plus 20% of the balance, capped at £800,000 for floating charges created on or after 6 April 2020 (£600,000 for older charges). Only then does the floating-charge holder get paid, and unsecured creditors take whatever remains. The lender responses to 2020's reordering were predictable and you will see them in Barclays' book: closer monitoring of tax arrears as a covenant and early-warning item, structuring towards fixed charges where the asset supports one, and a materially more conservative view of what a debenture is wor

docs.title: Personal guarantees: the last mile
docs.text: When the company's carcass is picked clean, the bank turns to the guarantor. Enforcement of a personal guarantee is procedurally simple — written demand, then county or High Court proceedings, then enforcement against the individual: charging orders over property, orders for sale in extremis, statutory demand and bankruptcy as the final lever. In practice it is slow, contested and partial. Guarantors dispute execution, allege misrepresentation, or simply have nothing left: the director's wealth was usually in the business, and the average guarantee now stands near £200,000 (Purbeck put the mean demand at roughly £194,000 in Q2 2025) against individuals whose main asset is a jointly owned family home. Realistic outcomes are negotiated settlements at a substantial discount, or instalment arrangements running years; full recovery is the exception. The conduct sensitivities are acute and post-GRG permanent. Enforcing against a family home, a retired guarantor, or a spouse who signed without independent advice is exactly the fact pattern that ends up in front of the Financial Ombudsman (guarantees by individuals can fall within its remit), in the press, or in Parliament — the FSB has campaigned loudly against personal-guarantee practice on small loans, and the FCA has reviewed lender behaviour at the perimeter. Banks therefore enforce PGs deliberately: vulnerability checks, settlement preference, and a visible reluctance to bankrupt. For the analyst, that restraint is a recovery h

docs.title: The numbers, and what they do to your provisions
docs.text: The Insolvency Service 's data tells you what the workout book actually faces. 2025 recorded 23,938 company insolvencies in England and Wales — near the historically elevated plateau of 2023–24. The mix is the message: 18,525 were CVLs (around three-quarters), 3,730 compulsory liquidations (the highest since 2012), just 1,495 administrations and 186 CVAs. One in every 190 registered companies entered insolvency in the year — a liquidation rate of 52.5 per 10,000. Sector concentration matters for a BB book: in the twelve months to November 2025, wholesale and retail (16%) plus accommodation and food services (14%) supplied roughly a third of all failures — consumer-facing, leasehold-heavy, labour-intensive sectors. By mid-2026 the tide had begun to ebb — June 2026's 1,845 insolvencies ran about 10% below June 2025 — but ebbing from a decade-high plateau still leaves a full workout pipeline. Now assemble the domino chain this module has been building. Trading deteriorates; arrears and breaches trigger a Business Support transfer; the workout strategy fork chooses between consensual turnaround and an insolvency route; the regime selected fixes the recovery path — going-concern premium via administration or pre-pack, break-up values via CVL; the waterfall applies HMRC's preference and the prescribed part before the floating charge; the shortfall chases the guarantor. Each step is an input to the Stage 3 DCF: scenario cash flows, probabilities, timelines, discounting. The chain en

docs.title: The rate that came down — and stopped
docs.text: The story you inherit in August 2026 is not a rate shock; it is a rate plateau. Bank Rate peaked at 5.25% in August 2023, sat there for a year, then descended in careful quarter-point steps — August and November 2024, then February, May, August and December 2025 — to 3.75%, where it has been parked ever since. The June 2026 hold went 7–2; the July 2026 hold went 6–3, and the dissenters wanted a rise . Markets still pencil in one or two cuts by year-end, but the honest reading is that the era of near-free money is not coming back. For a book of SME borrowers, 3.75% is not relief. It is the new floor. Why does a falling rate still hurt? Because of when the debt was written. The great mass of BB term lending — commercial mortgages, asset finance, the post-pandemic recovery borrowing — was priced between 2020 and 2021, when Bank Rate was 0.1%. Five-year fixes from that vintage matured into 2025 and 2026; what analysts called the refinancing wall did not collapse on the book in one quarter, it has been grinding through it maturity by maturity, repricing debt service at double or triple the old coupon. The symptoms are visible in the utilisation data: SME overdraft utilisation hit 49.3% in Q1 2026, the highest since early 2024, as firms borrowed to cover tax bills, energy, employment costs and — circularly — to refinance other debt. And the insolvency needle has not fallen with the rate. There were 23,938 company insolvencies in England and Wales in 2025 — essentially flat on 2024,

docs.title: The long tail of the bounce back book
docs.text: Six years after launch, the Bounce Back Loan Scheme is still the largest single legacy item on the BB radar. The government's repayment data as at 31 March 2026 shows £46.47 billion drawn across roughly 1.5 million facilities. By volume, 19.4% are fully repaid and 47.0% on schedule; 3.9% sit in arrears, 0.7% have defaulted but not yet been claimed, and the government guarantee has been settled on 28.3% of facilities. Read that last number again: more than a quarter of all bounce back loans, by count, have already ended in a settled guarantee claim . The December 2025 Covid Counter Fraud Commissioner's final report put fraud and error across the Covid support schemes at £10.9 billion, with BBLS singled out for its self-certified, no-checks design. What keeps this a forward radar item rather than a history lesson is Pay As You Grow . The original loans were six-year facilities drawn between May 2020 and March 2021, which would have run the book off by 2027. But PAYG let borrowers extend to ten years at the same 2.5% fixed rate, take payment holidays, or drop to interest-only for six months up to three times. A ten-year extension on a March 2021 drawdown matures in 2031. The British Business Bank confirms extension leaves the guarantee intact — but it also means the residual book is self-selected: the firms that extended are, on average, the firms that couldn't afford the six-year profile. The tail is long, thin, and adversely selected. Impairment Lens The 100% guarantee is an i

docs.title: Basel 3.1: the capital reshuffle behind SME pricing
docs.text: Capital rules are not impairment rules, but they set the price and supply of the credit whose losses you later count. Basel 3.1 is the UK's implementation of the final post-2008 capital package, and its timetable has been a moving target: near-final PRA rules landed in September 2024 with a January 2026 start; on 17 January 2025 the PRA, in consultation with HM Treasury, delayed implementation to 1 January 2027 , citing uncertainty over what the United States would do; final rules were published in January 2026, with the market-risk internal model piece pushed further to 2028. As of today the go-live is five months away, and it is real. The fight that matters for BB was over the SME supporting factor — the EU-inherited discount that scaled down risk weights on SME exposures and made small-business lending cheaper to hold. The PRA's original proposal simply deleted it, and lenders warned loudly that SME credit would reprice or retreat. The landing zone was a compromise: the supporting factor goes from Pillar 1, but the PRA introduced a firm-specific SME lending adjustment in Pillar 2A, designed to offset the aggregate capital impact (a parallel adjustment covers infrastructure). Alongside it, the Small Domestic Deposit Taker regime gives smaller banks a simplified framework — which shapes how the challengers who now write most SME flow will be capitalised. The catch is in the phrase firm-specific . A Pillar 1 factor was automatic, permanent and visible in pricing models; a Pil

docs.title: Plumbing: referrals, open finance, and the end of the PSR
docs.text: Three quieter structural stories set the data and payments environment BB will operate in. First, the Bank Referral Scheme — the 2016 statutory duty on major banks to refer declined SME credit applicants, with consent, to designated finance platforms (Funding Options, Funding Xchange, Alternative Business Funding and Business Finance Technology). Its conversion record has always been modest, and after a 2024 post-implementation review HM Treasury consulted again in October 2025. The May 2026 government response was a shrug with a twist: no legislative overhaul of the scheme itself, but an intention to expand the Commercial Credit Data Sharing regime so that entities beyond regulated banks can be designated. Translation — the state has stopped trying to fix referrals and started widening the data pipes instead. Second, open banking is graduating into open finance . The UK passed 16 million open banking users during 2025, and variable recurring payments already account for around 16% of open banking payment volumes. The commercial leap is commercial VRPs : a 31-firm vehicle, the UK Payments Initiative, was stood up at the end of 2025 to run the first commercial VRP scheme, with the first live payments expected from early 2026 across utilities, financial services and government use cases. HM Treasury legislation in 2026 will hand the FCA formal rule-making powers over the ecosystem. For BB, a business account that streams its transaction data and pays by VRP is a business the ba

docs.title: New money: private credit, B2B BNPL, embedded finance
docs.text: Follow the flow of new SME lending and you are no longer mostly watching the big banks. UK SME lending rose almost 10% to roughly £68 billion in 2025, and about 68% of it came from challenger and specialist banks or non-bank lenders — the third straight year the incumbents were the minority. Behind the challengers stands private credit : direct-lending funds pushing down from the mid-market into smaller tickets, banks responding with fund partnerships rather than balance-sheet competition, and structures like European direct-lending CLOs (Ares priced one in June 2025) giving the asset class term funding. The disintermediation that ate leveraged lending is now grazing on SME credit. The retail-facing face of the same trend is BNPL for business. UK B2B buy-now-pay-later volumes were estimated around US$13.7 billion in 2025, heading toward US$16.5 billion, with Kriya, Hokodo and iwoca 's iwocaPay embedding pay-later terms directly into B2B checkouts, procurement portals and accounting software — embedded finance replacing the paper invoice-discounting of old. The consolidation signal came in October 2025 when Allica Bank bought Kriya, promising £1 billion of deployment: regulated challenger balance sheets are becoming the funding layer under fintech distribution. Note the regulatory asymmetry: FCA regulation of consumer deferred payment credit went live on 15 July 2026 under PS26/1 — affordability checks, Ombudsman access, the lot — while B2B BNPL remains entirely outside the pe

docs.title: The fraud bill arrives: APP reimbursement
docs.text: On 7 October 2024 the Payment Systems Regulator switched on mandatory reimbursement for APP fraud — authorised push payment scams, where the victim is deceived into sending the money themselves. The rules are blunt: victims reimbursed up to £85,000 within five business days, cost split 50/50 between sending and receiving payment firms, covering Faster Payments and CHAPS. The cap was itself a late retreat — the original proposal was £415,000, cut after industry pressure — though the PSR maintains 99.8% of cases fall under £85,000. Between launch and June 2025, roughly £112 million went back to victims, about 88% of the money stolen in in-scope scams. An independent one-year review began in October 2025, testing the cap, the 50/50 split and the customer-caution exception, with findings due in 2026/27 — landing on the FCA's desk as it absorbs the PSR. The BB angle is the scope line. "Consumers" here includes micro-enterprises (broadly, under 10 staff and €2m turnover) and small charities — so the bottom of the BB book is inside the protection, while the standard business account above the threshold is not. That cliff-edge matters twice over. A protected microenterprise that loses £60,000 to an invoice-redirection scam gets it back and survives; an unprotected small business one size up absorbs the hit — and invoice fraud losses of that scale are precisely the kind of one-off cash event that turns a performing borrower into a watchlist case. docs.text: The signature section. Everything above, compressed into a ranked watchlist — each item tied to the model input it will actually move between now and mid-2028. The rate plateau meets the last of the refinancing wall. Bank Rate stuck near 3.75% while 2020–21 vintage fixes keep maturing means debt-service repricing continues with no offsetting macro improvement — the purest PD driver on the board, and a forward-looking-economics calibration problem because no scenario variable is moving. The BBLS/PAYG tail, 2026–2031. An adversely selected residual book with guarantee-settled claims already at 28% of facilities: near-zero LGD on the loans themselves, but a live staging and cross-default signal for every unguaranteed facility beside them — and a guarantee-voiding operational risk that belongs in a PMA discussion. Basel 3.1 go-live, 1 January 2027. Supporting factor out of Pillar 1, discretionary adjustment in Pillar 2A: expect repricing and selective retreat at the margin, so refusal-at-refinance becomes a default pathway — PD for the weakest cohort, EAD as limits are managed down ahead of the date. Compulsory liquidations at a 13-year high. Creditor- and HMRC-initiated windings-up shorten the runway from stress to terminal event — faster Stage 3 inflow, and LGD timing effects as compulsory processes recover less than negotiated exits. docs.title: Business current account (BCA)
docs.text: The transactional bank account through which a business routes receipts, payments and wages. The anchor BB product: source of cheap deposits, fee income, cross-sale, and — critically for credit risk — live behavioural data on trading health via account turnover and limit usage.

docs.title: SME
docs.text: Small and medium-sized enterprise, conventionally a firm with fewer than 250 employees. UK SMEs numbered ~5.68 million at the start of 2025 — 99.85% of all businesses — employing ~16.9 million people. Banks sub-segment them by annual turnover, with 'business banking' boundaries ranging from ~£2m to £25m.

docs.title: Sole trader
docs.text: An unincorporated business owned by one individual with no legal separation between personal and business assets — the owner is personally liable for all debts. Around 56% of UK businesses; most employ nobody. For lenders, effectively consumer credit wearing a trading name.

docs.title: Overdraft
docs.text: A revolving borrowing limit on the BCA, repayable on demand, funding day-to-day working capital. Usually unsecured or floating-charge secured at the small end. Risk is EAD-shaped: utilisation climbs towards and through the limit as a firm approaches default.

docs.title: Term loan
docs.text: A fixed advance repaid on an amortising schedule, typically over one to ten-plus years, funding expansion, acquisition or refinancing. EAD is predictable; risk concentrates in PD — whether cash flows survive the term — and in LGD where the loan is unsecured.

docs.title: Commercial mortgage
docs.text: A long-term loan (typically 15–25 years) secured on business premises or investment property. LGD is driven by the commercial property cycle, which is more volatile and less liquid than residential; for investment property, tenant quality can matter as much as borrower quality.

docs.title: Asset finance
docs.text: Hire purchase and leasing used to fund vehicles, plant and equipment, with the asset as security and title often retained by the funder. LGD turns on used-asset resale values: 'hard' assets with liquid secondary markets recover well; bespoke 'soft' assets do not.

docs.title: Invoice finance
docs.text: Lending advanced against unpaid trade invoices — typically 80–90% of face value — via factoring or invoice discounting. Self-liquidating: debtor payments repay the advance, so EAD is short-dated and LGD modest. Tail risk is fraud: fresh-air invoices and double-financing.

docs.title: Merchant acquiring
docs.text: Processing card payments on behalf of businesses, earning a margin per transaction — Barclays operates through Barclaycard Payments. Carries contingent credit risk: if a merchant fails after taking payment but before delivering goods or services, chargebacks fall on the acquirer.

docs.title: Small corporate
docs.text: A firm at the top of the BB pyramid — near the segment boundary (£6.5m turnover at Barclays) — with proper financial management, fuller accounts and multi-product needs. Large enough for manual underwriting and individual impairment assessment; small enough to lack capital-markets access.

docs.title: Turnover segmentation
docs.text: Dividing business customers into bank segments by annual turnover. Boundaries vary by bank — Barclays moves firms to its UK Corporate Bank at £6.5m; Lloyds runs tiers at £3m and £25m; NatWest's business segment ends near £2m — so cross-bank 'SME book' comparisons rarely compare like with like.

docs.title: BCA turnover
docs.text: The gross credit flow through a firm's business current account — a live, hard-to-falsify proxy for trading revenue, available months before filed accounts. A core input to BB behavioural PD models and SICR triggers, but noisy and endogenous: firms can route receipts elsewhere.

docs.title: Goldsmith bankers
docs.text: Seventeenth-century London goldsmiths who took deposits for safekeeping, issued receipts that circulated as money, and lent against them — the direct ancestors of English deposit banking. Barclays traces its 1690 origins to the goldsmith-banking partnership of John Freame and Thomas Gould on Lombard Street.

docs.title: Clearing banks
docs.text: The large joint-stock banks that settled payments through the London Clearing House — historically the Big Five, later Big Four (Barclays, Lloyds, Midland/HSBC, NatWest). They dominated England and Wales business banking for a century, operating as a de facto oligopoly in deposits, money transmission and SME credit.

docs.title: Interest-rate cartel
docs.text: The clearing banks' formal agreement to fix deposit rates and move lending rates in step with Bank Rate, tolerated by the authorities in exchange for compliance with credit controls. Abolished by Competition and Credit Control in 1971.

docs.title: Macmillan gap
docs.text: The structural shortfall in long-term finance for small firms identified by the Macmillan Committee in 1931 — too small for capital markets, too risky for rationed bank credit. The founding diagnosis of UK SME finance policy, rediscovered by successive inquiries ever since.

docs.title: Competition and Credit Control (1971)
docs.text: Bank of England reform of September 1971 abolishing lending ceilings and the clearing-bank cartel, switching credit control from rationing to price (interest rates and special deposits). Unleashed the Barber boom — broad money up ~72% by end-1973 — and set up the secondary banking crisis.

docs.title: Secondary banking crisis (1973–75)
docs.text: Collapse of lightly supervised, wholesale-funded 'fringe' banks that had lent heavily against commercial property after 1971 liberalisation. Rate spikes and a property crash triggered funding runs; twenty-six institutions needed support. The template UK cycle: liberalisation, property concentration, collateral collapse, losses.

docs.title: Lifeboat operation
docs.text: The Bank of England-orchestrated support pool, launched December 1973 and funded ~90% by the clearing banks, that lent up to £1.3bn to twenty-six failing secondary banks to contain the 1973–75 crisis. An early lesson that clearers pay for systemic property-lending excess even when others originate it.

docs.title: Big Bang (1986)
docs.text: The 27 October 1986 deregulation of the London Stock Exchange: fixed commissions abolished, broker/jobber separation ended, outside ownership permitted, screen trading introduced. Pulled clearing banks into investment banking and, via disintermediation of large corporates, pushed their lending down-market toward SMEs and property.

docs.title: BZW
docs.text: Barclays de Zoete Wedd — the investment bank Barclays assembled at Big Bang from broker de Zoete & Bevan and jobber Wedd Durlacher. Emblem of the era's diversion of clearers' capital and attention from business banking; largely sold to Credit Suisse in 1997, with remnants becoming Barclays Capital.

docs.title: Overdraft culture
docs.text: The historical UK pattern of financing SMEs through on-demand overdrafts secured on property and personal guarantees rather than term debt. Cheap and flexible in benign times; procyclical in downturns, because banks can cut limits and call facilities exactly when borrowers are weakest — as in 1990–93.

docs.title: Small banks crisis (1991–94)
docs.text: The failure of roughly a quarter of the UK's small and medium-sized banks within three years of BCCI's July 1991 closure, as wholesale funding fled weaker names amid recession and property losses. The Bank of England provided discreet liquidity support to prevent contagion to larger institutions.

docs.title: Demutualisation
docs.text: Conversion of mutual building societies into shareholder-owned banks under the Building Societies Act 1986 — Abbey National (1989), then Halifax, Woolwich, Alliance & Leicester and Northern Rock (1997). Transformed mortgage and savings competition while leaving SME banking concentration untouched; several converts were later absorbed by the clearers.

docs.title: Cruickshank Report (2000)
docs.text: Don Cruickshank's Treasury-commissioned review of UK banking competition, published 20 March 2000. Found concentrated markets, switching barriers, bank control of payments, and persistent excess profits from personal and SME customers — and triggered the Competition Commission's SME banking inquiry.

docs.title: Competition Commission SME banking report (2002)
docs.text: The March 2002 inquiry finding a 'complex monopoly' in SME banking: the big four held ~90% of the market and their parallel practices restricted price competition. Remedies were behavioural — interest on SME current accounts (base minus 2.5%) or free banking from 2003, plus anti-bundling undertakings, the last released in December 2025.

docs.title: Project Merlin
docs.text: February 2011 agreement between the Treasury and five major banks committing 'capacity and willingness' for £190bn gross new business lending in 2011, £76bn to SMEs. Overall target exceeded; SME target missed by about £1bn. Criticised for counting gross lending while net SME credit kept shrinking, with no penalty mechanism.

docs.title: Funding for Lending Scheme
docs.text: Bank of England/Treasury scheme (2012–18) giving banks cheap funding priced off their net lending. The April 2013 extension skewed incentives to SMEs — up to £10 of drawings per £1 of net SME lending. Revived mortgage pricing and crushed savings rates; evaluations found no identifiable direct boost to SME credit.

docs.title: Global Restructuring Group
docs.text: RBS's division for distressed business customers; around 12,000 SMEs passed through it 2008–13. The FCA's s.166 review found widespread inappropriate treatment, with about one in six customers materially harmed by the bank. No enforcement followed — commercial lending sat outside the regulatory perimeter. RBS set aside £400m for fee refunds and complaints.

docs.title: Interest-Rate Hedging Products
docs.text: Swaps, caps, collars and structured collars sold alongside SME loans 2001–11, often as a lending condition. When rates collapsed, fixed payments and huge break costs crippled borrowers. An FSA-brokered review saw nine banks pay over £2.2bn redress on some 14,000 accepted offers; a 'sophistication test' excluded roughly 10,000 sales.

docs.title: CMA 2016 Market Investigation
docs.text: Competition and Markets Authority investigation into personal current account and SME banking, final report August 2016. Found weak competition driven by customer inertia. Remedies were behavioural, not structural: the open banking API mandate, published service-quality league tables, overdraft alerts and charge caps, and SME loan-price transparency tools.

docs.title: Banking Competition Remedies
docs.text: Independent body created in 2018 to administer RBS's £775m state-aid alternative remedies package: a £425m Capability & Innovation Fund of grants and £350m for incentivised switching of SME customers. Agreed with the European Commission in 2017 after the Williams & Glyn divestment was abandoned.

docs.title: Incentivised Switching Scheme
docs.text: BCR scheme (2019–21) paying dowries to challenger banks for each former Williams & Glyn SME customer switching their business current account: £275m for dowries plus £75m towards customer costs. Delivered 69,135 switches against ambitions of up to 120,000; £250.9m (over 91%) disbursed. Starling switched the most.

docs.title: Williams & Glyn
docs.text: The 300-plus-branch SME-heavy business RBS was ordered to divest as an EU state-aid condition of its £45.5bn bailout. A Santander sale collapsed in 2012; standalone-bank plans consumed over £1.5bn, mostly on IT separation. Abandoned in 2017 and replaced by the £775m alternative remedies package.

docs.title: Tomlinson Report
docs.text: November 2013 report by Lawrence Tomlinson, entrepreneur in residence at the business department, alleging RBS GRG pushed viable SMEs into distress via revaluations and fees, with the bank's West Register arm acquiring their assets. Triggered the FCA's skilled-person review of GRG.

docs.title: Section 166 Review
docs.text: A 'skilled person' review under s.166 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000: the regulator requires an independent expert report on a firm's conduct or systems. Promontory, assisted by Mazars, conducted the GRG s.166 review, delivering its report to the FCA in September 2016.

docs.title: Capability & Innovation Fund
docs.text: The £425m grant arm of the BCR package. Pool A (2019): Metro Bank £120m, Starling £100m, ClearBank with Tide £60m. Pool B: Nationwide £50m, Investec £15m, Co-op Bank £15m. Pool C: £10m grants; Pool D: £5m grants. Metro and Nationwide each returned £50m, recycled as Pool E in 2020.

docs.title: Swift Review
docs.text: John Swift QC's lessons-learned review of the IRHP redress scheme, published December 2021. Found most in-scope customers likely did better inside the scheme than outside, but criticised the exclusion of 'sophisticated' customers and weak FCA governance. The FCA declined to reopen redress; courts upheld that in 2023.

docs.title: TSB Carve-out
docs.text: Lloyds' EU-mandated divestment (Project Verde). After the Co-op purchase collapsed in 2013, TSB launched, IPO'd in 2014 and was sold to Sabadell in 2015 for £1.7bn. Its 2018 IT migration locked out up to 1.9m customers, drawing £48.65m in fines. Santander's £2.65bn acquisition completed 30 April 2026.

docs.title: West Register
docs.text: RBS's property-investment arm, which could acquire assets sold by distressed customers managed in GRG — the conflict of interest at the heart of the Tomlinson allegations. The s.166 review did not find a deliberate asset-stripping strategy, but the optics led banks to bar workout units from buying customer assets.

docs.title: Bounce Back Loan Scheme (BBLS)
docs.text: COVID emergency scheme (May 2020–March 2021): loans of £2k–£50k, capped at 25% of turnover, 2.5% fixed, six-year term, 100% government guarantee, self-certified eligibility, no credit checks. £46.5bn drawn across ~1.5m facilities. The defining book of modern BB impairment.

docs.title: Coronavirus Business Interruption Loan Scheme (CBILS)
docs.text: COVID scheme (March 2020–March 2021) for businesses with turnover up to £45m: facilities up to £5m across loans, overdrafts, invoice and asset finance, 80% government guarantee, lender underwriting retained, government-paid first-year interest and fees, no personal guarantees below £250k. £25.8bn drawn; far better performance than BBLS.

docs.title: Coronavirus Large Business Interruption Loan Scheme (CLBILS)
docs.text: COVID scheme for firms with turnover above £45m: facilities eventually up to £200m, 80% guarantee, dividend and executive-pay restrictions on larger facilities. £4.5bn drawn, ~96% fully repaid by March 2026 — negligible for impairment purposes.

docs.title: Recovery Loan Scheme (RLS)
docs.text: Successor guarantee scheme launched April 2021. Iteration 1: 80% guarantee, up to £10m. From January 2022: 70%, £2m cap, SMEs only. From August 2022: no COVID-impact test required — a standing SME guarantee programme. Renamed the Growth Guarantee Scheme in July 2024.

docs.title: Growth Guarantee Scheme (GGS)
docs.text: The RLS's current form (from July 2024): 70% government guarantee on facilities up to £2m, full commercial underwriting and pricing, personal guarantees permitted excluding principal residences. Extended to March 2030 at the June 2025 Spending Review; ~£3.6bn delivered through 70+ lenders by March 2026.

docs.title: Pay As You Grow (PAYG)
docs.text: Built-in BBLS repayment flexibility, exercisable at borrower option without lender assessment: term extension from six to ten years at the same 2.5% rate; six months interest-only (up to three times); one six-month repayment holiday. Used by ~37% of BBLS facilities; guarantee unaffected. Stretched and flattened arrears emergence.

docs.title: British Business Bank (BBB)
docs.text: State economic-development bank, owned by the Department for Business and Trade. Accredits lenders to the guarantee schemes, sets and audits scheme rules, administers the Scheme Portal (system of record), and processes guarantee claims on behalf of the Secretary of State as guarantor.

docs.title: Guarantee claim
docs.text: The process by which a lender recovers guaranteed losses: after default, the lender completes required recovery steps under scheme rules, submits the claim via the BBB Scheme Portal, and is reimbursed the guaranteed share. Post-settlement recoveries are remitted to government pro rata. £12.98bn settled across the COVID schemes by March 2026.

docs.title: Self-certification
docs.text: The BBLS application basis: borrowers attested their own turnover, COVID impact and eligibility on a short form, with lenders explicitly relieved of credit and affordability assessment (fraud/AML/KYC checks only). The scheme's core speed mechanism — and its core fraud vulnerability.

docs.title: Business Interruption Payment (BIP)
docs.text: Government payment covering the first twelve months of interest (and, for CBILS, fees) on COVID scheme facilities, paid directly to the lender so borrowers faced no cost in year one. Combined with the BBLS capital holiday, it delayed the first true affordability test to 2021–22.

docs.title: Guarantee removal
docs.text: Retrospective withdrawal of the government guarantee from a scheme facility, typically after BBB audit finds scheme-rule breaches or data errors. £1.16bn across 14,757 loans removed by March 2026. Converts a state-backed exposure into ordinary unsecured lending — an operational event with an LGD-cliff impairment consequence.

docs.title: Fraud flag
docs.text: A lender's marker on a scheme facility suspected of fraudulent application or use, reported through the BBB Scheme Portal. As at March 2026, £1.88bn of BBLS drawn value (4.04%) was flagged — well below early official estimates of 11% (£4.9bn). Flagged loans follow counter-fraud recovery routes distinct from ordinary collections.

docs.title: Barclays UK
docs.text: Barclays' ring-fenced division (legal entity Barclays Bank UK PLC), holding UK retail and small-business banking. Reports three segments: Personal Banking, Barclaycard Consumer UK, and Business Banking. End-2025: £215.6bn loans, £244.7bn deposits, 20.7% RoTE. Business Banking clients hand off to the UK Corporate Bank above ~£6.5m turnover.

docs.title: Eagle Labs
docs.text: Barclays' national incubator network for tech start-ups, launched 2015, offering workspace, mentoring and growth programmes. Delivered the government's £12.09m Digital Growth Grant (2023–25) supporting 22,000+ businesses, 80% outside London. Strategically an origination funnel and franchise asset — it holds no credit exposure itself.

docs.title: Barclaycard Payments
docs.text: Barclays' merchant acquiring business — among the top two UK acquirers, processing c.8.7bn transactions annually (as at 2025). Historically a key SME differentiator and early-warning data source. Since April 2025, subject to a Brookfield partnership with a staged path toward Brookfield majority ownership.

docs.title: Coverage ratio
docs.text: Impairment allowance divided by gross exposure, overall or by stage. Barclays UK end-2025 markers: retail credit cards 4.3% total coverage, mortgages of the order of 0.1%, group c.1.2%. For BB, guarantees and secured/unsecured mix distort the blend — always decompose before comparing across books.

docs.title: ARA (Annual Report and Accounts)
docs.text: A bank's statutory annual disclosure. For BB analysis, the Barclays Bank UK PLC ARA matters most: it carries the ring-fenced bank's credit risk section, staging and coverage tables, and government-scheme commentary. Quarterly results announcements (RAs) give the interim segment view.

docs.title: Ring-fencing
docs.text: UK regime (in force 2019, from the Financial Services (Banking Reform) Act 2013) requiring large banks to separate core retail and SME deposit-taking into an independently capitalised entity, insulated from investment banking. Business Banking sits inside Barclays' ring-fenced bank, Barclays Bank UK PLC.

docs.title: UK Corporate Bank
docs.text: Barclays division (one of five since the February 2024 reorganisation) serving companies above roughly £6.5m annual turnover with lending, cash management, trade and FX. The upper boundary of Business Banking: larger, chunkier credits — and their impairment — are disclosed here, not in BB.

docs.title: Loan loss rate
docs.text: Annualised credit impairment charge as basis points of gross loans. Barclays UK: 14bps (FY23), 16bps (FY24), 18bps (FY25) — mortgage-dominated, hence far below group through-the-cycle guidance of 50–60bps. Group H1 2026: 62bps. The drift matters more than the level.

docs.title: Brookfield partnership
docs.text: April 2025 agreement on Barclays' UK merchant acquiring business: Barclays invests c.£400m over three years to modernise the platform; Brookfield Asset Management leads transformation and holds an option to acquire roughly 70–80% between years three and seven — a staged majority exit from acquiring.

docs.title: Digital Growth Grant
docs.text: £12.09m UK government grant awarded to Barclays Eagle Labs to deliver start-up and scale-up support from April 2023 to March 2025 — over 22,000 businesses targeted, at least 80% outside London. Controversial at award (displacing Tech Nation), it cemented Eagle Labs' ecosystem role.

docs.title: Starling Bank
docs.text: Digital bank founded 2014; the largest BCR-era challenger, holding c.10% of UK SME business current accounts with £714m revenue in FY2025. Deposit-rich, lending-light. Booked a £28.2m provision in FY2025 after voluntarily removing the government guarantee from BBLS loans whose origination checks failed scheme conditions.

docs.title: Tide
docs.text: E-money business-banking platform — not a UK bank — holding client funds via ClearBank. Roughly 900,000 UK members by mid-2026, a self-reported c.15% of UK SMEs by count. Monetises payments and subscriptions; credit mostly originated through partners. Its share metric counts businesses, not lending or deposit value.

docs.title: Allica Bank
docs.text: Full-service digital bank for established SMEs (roughly 10–250 employees). Lending grew 23% to £3.7bn in 2025 — mostly commercial mortgages plus asset, growth and bridging finance — funded by £5.7bn of savings deposits. Third consecutive profitable year; the standing example of relationship underwriting rebuilt on modern rails.

docs.title: OakNorth
docs.text: UK bank lending £250k–£100m to property and trading businesses; £7.2bn of facilities and £223m pre-tax profit in 2025. Cumulative principal losses of 0.045% (£6.9m) across its first decade — the canonical low-default portfolio. Sells its underwriting and monitoring stack to other banks as ON Credit Intelligence.

docs.title: Funding Circle
docs.text: UK SME lending platform that pioneered marketplace lending, then pivoted: US exit, and growth via FlexiPay working-capital lines held on its own balance sheet. In 2025: £3.0bn under management, £2.5bn of credit extended, £20.3m pre-tax profit. Proof that originate-to-distribute relocates credit risk rather than removing it.

docs.title: iwoca
docs.text: Data-driven lender of short-term unsecured working capital to small businesses; £1.3bn lent across 58,000 loans in 2025, up 60%. Distributes through embedded API partnerships — accountancy software, payment firms, neobanks — reaching c.3m businesses. Wholesale-funded via facilities such as a £250m Waterfall Asset Management line.

docs.title: Mettle
docs.text: NatWest's standalone app-based business current account for sole traders and small limited companies — the incumbent's defensive answer to Starling and Tide, run as a separate brand with fee-free accounts and integrated accounting software.

docs.title: Tyl
docs.text: NatWest's merchant-acquiring service, launched 2019, offering card terminals and payment processing to SMEs. Among the fastest-growing UK bank-owned acquirers; entered a technology partnership with Endava in 2026. Gives NatWest the card-takings data stream that fintech acquirers use for lending.

docs.title: Kinetic
docs.text: HSBC UK's app-based business banking platform for small businesses — account opening, overdrafts and small loans delivered digitally. HSBC's vehicle for defending the small-SME end of its franchise while its core appetite concentrates on internationally trading firms.

docs.title: Shawbrook
docs.text: Specialist UK bank funded by retail savings and securitisation; £19.2bn loan book at end-2025 (up 16%), including £4.4bn of SME lending alongside real-estate and retail mortgages. Acquired ThinCats to deepen mid-market SME reach and returned to the London Stock Exchange.

docs.title: Aldermore
docs.text: Specialist bank owned by South Africa's FirstRand, focused on asset finance, invoice finance and commercial mortgages for SMEs, funded largely by retail savings. Accredited under the Growth Guarantee Scheme, having previously lent under the Recovery Loan Scheme.

docs.title: Zempler Bank
docs.text: Small-business bank, formerly Cashplus, with c.170,000 business accounts and three consecutive years of profit to FY2025. Embeds iwoca's lending inside its own accounts rather than building a large credit book — a working example of the embedded-credit pattern among account-first challengers.

docs.title: ThinCats
docs.text: Specialist lender providing bespoke, typically larger-ticket funding to established, growth-focused mid-sized SMEs, originated through advisers and its own regional team. Acquired by Shawbrook in 2025, extending the bank's reach into relationship-underwritten mid-market credit.

docs.title: Marketplace lending
docs.text: Originate-to-distribute model: a platform originates loans, sells them to institutional investors and retains servicing fees, holding little or no credit risk itself. Risk is relocated, not removed — when investor demand or economics shift, originators pivot to balance-sheet lending and the ECL comes home.

docs.title: Relationship lending
docs.text: Underwriting built on soft information a relationship manager accumulates about a business and its owners over time — character, competence, local context. Powerful for opaque SMEs but expensive and unscalable; largely stripped out of UK banking as credit decisions were centralised away from branches.

docs.title: Transactional-data lending
docs.text: Underwriting from the live flow of a business's current-account transactions — receipts, payments, balances — rather than financial statements. The dominant modern BB technology: timely, unfakeable, and the foundation of behavioural scoring. Open banking extended it to lenders who don't hold the account.

docs.title: Financial-statement lending
docs.text: Underwriting from a company's accounts: ratio analysis of profitability, gearing, interest cover and asset quality. Works for larger SMEs with audited, timely numbers; degrades badly for small companies whose public filings are abbreviated, unaudited and up to two years stale.

docs.title: Companies House
docs.text: The UK registrar of companies — the free public record of incorporations, directors, filed accounts and registered charges. BB underwriting's baseline data source, weakened by small-company filing exemptions and nine-month filing lags. ECCTA reforms added director identity verification (November 2025); fuller accounts reform is deferred to 2028.

docs.title: Filleted accounts
docs.text: Accounts a small company files at Companies House with the profit and loss account (and directors' report) removed — legally showing the public a balance sheet but no trading performance. Available to companies under the small-company thresholds (from April 2025: £15m turnover, £7.5m balance sheet, 50 employees).

docs.title: SIC code
docs.text: Standard Industrial Classification code self-declared at incorporation to describe a company's activity. Drives banks' sector segmentation, concentration limits and scenario mapping despite being frequently inaccurate and rarely updated — a shaky foundation load-bearing far more risk infrastructure than it deserves.

docs.title: Working-capital cycle
docs.text: The time between cash leaving a business and coming back: stock days plus debtor days minus creditor days. Positive cycles (builders, manufacturers) create permanent funding needs; negative cycles (pubs, retailers) generate float. Most SME failures are working-capital failures — profitable businesses that ran out of cash.

docs.title: Behavioural scoring
docs.text: Monthly statistical scoring of a business from its current-account conduct — turnover trends, excesses, unpaid items, balance volatility. Outperforms financial-statement models because it is current. In BB it drives limit management, watchlist entry and, critically, IFRS 9 SICR triggers and Stage 2 migration.

docs.title: Open banking
docs.text: The CMA-mandated API regime (live 2018) letting authorised third parties access bank-account data with customer consent. Passed 15 million UK users by mid-2026. In SME underwriting it lets challengers like iwoca and Tide read applicants' transaction histories — commoditising the incumbent's oldest data advantage.

docs.title: Personal guarantee
docs.text: A director's personal promise to repay company debt if the company cannot — converting limited liability back into personal exposure. Valued as both signal (willingness reveals the director's private confidence) and security, though recoveries are slow, contested and limited by the guarantor's actual wealth.

docs.title: Debenture
docs.text: The standard bank security document taking fixed and floating charges over all of a company's assets, registered at Companies House. Gives the lender priority claims and the power to appoint an administrator, but its floating-charge element is eroded by preferential creditors and the prescribed part.

docs.title: Fixed charge
docs.text: Security attached to specific, identifiable assets — typically property or plant — which the company cannot sell or deal with without the lender's consent. Fixed-charge holders sit at the top of the insolvency waterfall, paid from their asset ahead of preferential creditors and the prescribed part.

docs.title: Floating charge
docs.text: Security hovering over a company's circulating assets — stock, debtors, work in progress — which the business trades freely until insolvency crystallises the charge over whatever remains. Recoveries are diluted by insolvency costs, preferential creditors (including uncapped HMRC claims since 2020) and the prescribed part.

docs.title: Prescribed part
docs.text: The statutory carve-out from floating-charge realisations for unsecured creditors under s176A Insolvency Act 1986: 50% of the first £10,000 plus 20% of the remainder, capped at £800,000 for charges created on or after 6 April 2020. A direct, legislated reduction in the bank's floating-charge recovery.

docs.title: IFRS 9
docs.text: The accounting standard governing classification, measurement and impairment of financial instruments. Its expected-loss model forces provisions against SME lending before default. In Business Banking, its judgment-heavy corners — qualitative SICR, individual assessment, guarantee treatment, overlays — dominate the reported number far more than in retail.

docs.title: Expected credit loss (ECL)
docs.text: The probability-weighted present value of cash shortfalls over 12 months (Stage 1) or lifetime (Stages 2–3). In BB it is assembled from coarser models, a larger share of case-by-case judgment, and proportionally bigger post-model adjustments than its retail equivalent.

docs.title: Probability of default (PD)
docs.text: The likelihood of default over a 12-month or lifetime horizon. Retail PDs come from dense behavioural and bureau data; BB PDs above the micro end come from sparse default histories, expert-judgment grades and explicit margins of conservatism — making calibration, not rank-ordering, the hard problem.

docs.title: Loss given default (LGD)
docs.text: The share of exposure lost after recoveries. In BB it is driven by security packages — fixed and floating charges, debentures, personal guarantees — realisation costs and timelines, and, on Covid-scheme lending, government guarantees that can push effective LGD towards zero.

docs.title: Exposure at default (EAD)
docs.text: The predicted balance outstanding at default. Harder in BB than retail: overdrafts and revolving working-capital limits draw down as firms deteriorate, so credit conversion factors must capture a struggling business's tendency to use every pound of headroom before failing.

docs.title: Significant increase in credit risk (SICR)
docs.text: The Stage 1 to Stage 2 trigger. In BB it rests less on quantitative PD deltas and more on events — watchlist entry, covenant breach, BCA turnover collapse, sector flags — with the 30-days-past-due backstop as a late-arriving safety net rather than a primary signal.

docs.title: Staging
docs.text: Allocation of exposures to Stage 1 (12-month ECL), Stage 2 (lifetime ECL) or Stage 3 (credit-impaired). BB staging migrates in lumps, driven by discrete events and committee decisions, rather than the smooth score-driven monthly flows of a retail book.

docs.title: Stage 2
docs.text: Exposures whose credit risk has increased significantly since origination, carrying lifetime ECL. In BB, Stage 2 is populated heavily by qualitative triggers — watchlist entries, covenant breaches, sector flags — so its size and coverage can step-change when a committee re-grades a sector.

docs.title: Stage 3
docs.text: Credit-impaired exposures — the IFRS 9 analogue of default. In BB, larger Stage 3 cases leave the collective models entirely and are individually assessed through discounted-cash-flow workouts, making the Stage 3 charge lumpy and single-name driven.

docs.title: Individually assessed
docs.text: Provisioning a specific exposure on its own facts — bespoke recovery strategies, cash flows and probability weights — instead of modelled parameters. Triggered above a house exposure threshold or where fraud, litigation or complex security makes modelled outputs meaningless.

docs.title: Collective assessment
docs.text: Modelled ECL for pools of exposures sharing risk characteristics — product, size band, sector, grade. The default treatment for the SME mass market, where accounts are numerous and individually small enough for statistical parameters to be meaningful.

docs.title: Post-model adjustment (PMA)
docs.text: A quantified amendment to modelled ECL for risks the models miss — sector stress, insolvency lag, guarantee-claim risk, refinance affordability. BB books carry proportionally more PMA than retail because the underlying models are coarser and event risk larger; the PRA repeatedly probes their completeness and governance.

docs.title: Overlay
docs.text: Umbrella term for management adjustments layered onto modelled ECL, often used interchangeably with PMA; some banks reserve overlay for economics- or scenario-level adjustments and PMA for model-deficiency fixes. Either way it demands quantification, a release condition and an audit trail — or it is a cookie jar.

docs.title: Low default portfolio
docs.text: A portfolio with too few observed defaults to calibrate PD statistically — mid-corporates, larger SMEs, specialised lending. Forces reliance on expert-judgment rating scales, external benchmarks, slotting-like category approaches and explicit margins of conservatism, leaving the level of ECL genuinely uncertain even when rank-ordering is sound.

docs.title: Integral guarantee
docs.text: A guarantee treated as part of a loan's contractual terms, so expected claims enter ECL cash flows and reduce LGD. UK banks judged the BBLS/CBILS guarantees integral — created at origination under scheme rules and held by the lender — producing stressed guaranteed books with near-zero coverage.

docs.title: Watchlist
docs.text: The governed register of exposures showing early deterioration, fed by relationship managers, monitoring triggers and account conduct. Entry usually constitutes SICR, so watchlist governance is staging governance: a committee decision with a direct lifetime-ECL consequence.

docs.title: Covenant breach
docs.text: Failure of a contractual financial test — leverage, interest cover, loan-to-value, minimum net worth. A canonical BB SICR trigger with no retail equivalent; whether waived or enforced, a breach signals the borrower's finances have left the envelope the bank underwrote.

docs.title: DCF workout
docs.text: Individual Stage 3 provisioning by projecting cash flows under alternative recovery strategies — trade-out, consensual sale, insolvency — probability-weighting them and discounting at the original effective interest rate. The provision is exposure less the weighted present value of recoveries.

docs.title: Forward-looking economics
docs.text: Incorporating macroeconomic forecasts into ECL through multiple weighted scenarios. For SME books the load-bearing variables are GDP, corporate insolvency rates, base rate and CRE indices — not the HPI-and-unemployment pairing that dominates retail models — with insolvency lag the defining design problem.

docs.title: Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL)
docs.text: Director-initiated wind-up of an insolvent company: shareholders resolve to liquidate, an insolvency practitioner sells assets at break-up values and distributes via the statutory waterfall. The dominant UK insolvency route (~75% of cases). Unsecured recoveries are typically pence in the pound or nil; final distributions take one to two years.

docs.title: Compulsory liquidation
docs.text: Court-ordered winding-up on a creditor's petition — frequently HMRC's. Slower than a CVL (months from petition to order) and typically lower-recovery, as the business has deteriorated untreated. 2025's total of 3,730 was the highest since 2012, driven by HMRC's post-Covid return to enforcement.

docs.title: Administration
docs.text: Insolvency regime with a rescue-first purpose hierarchy and a moratorium on enforcement. A qualifying floating-charge holder can appoint out of court. Lasts twelve months (extendable); going-concern sales can materially beat break-up values, supporting the strongest secured recoveries. Around 1,495 UK administrations in 2025.

docs.title: Pre-pack administration
docs.text: An administration where the business sale is negotiated before appointment and completed immediately after, preserving goodwill and jobs at the cost of transparency. Since 30 April 2021, connected-party sales within the first eight weeks require creditor approval or an independent evaluator's opinion.

docs.title: Evaluator
docs.text: Independent reviewer created by the 2021 pre-pack regulations. Provides a written opinion on whether a connected-party disposal in administration is reasonable. An adverse opinion does not block the sale — the administrator may proceed but must explain the decision to creditors.

docs.title: Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA)
docs.text: A deal with unsecured creditors, approved by 75% by value, under which the company trades on and pays contributions over typically three to five years. Cannot bind secured creditors without consent. Now rare (186 in 2025) and fragile — historically roughly half fail into a subsequent insolvency.

docs.title: Part 26A restructuring plan
docs.text: Court-sanctioned compromise introduced by CIGA 2020 that can bind secured creditors and cram down entire dissenting classes if no member is worse off than in the relevant alternative. Powerful but costly — two hearings and seven-figure fees keep it a large-cap and upper-mid-market tool.

docs.title: Cross-class cram-down
docs.text: The Part 26A mechanism letting the court sanction a restructuring plan despite a whole class voting against it, provided dissenters are no worse off than in the relevant alternative and one in-the-money class approves. It removes the veto that dissenting creditor classes hold under schemes and CVAs.

docs.title: Standalone moratorium
docs.text: CIGA 2020 breathing-space procedure: 20 business days (extendable to 40, further with consent or court order) under a monitor, staying most creditor action while directors stay in control. Take-up is minimal — debts under financial services contracts are excluded from the payment holiday, so bank debt must still be serviced.

docs.title: HMRC preferential status
docs.text: Since 1 December 2020 (Finance Act 2020), HMRC ranks as secondary preferential creditor for taxes collected on its behalf — VAT, PAYE, employee NICs, CIS — ahead of floating-charge holders and unsecured creditors, uncapped and without age limit. Corporation tax remains unsecured. A direct hit to floating-charge LGD.

docs.title: Business Support Unit
docs.text: A bank's specialist turnaround function for deteriorating business customers — restructuring facilities, commissioning independent business reviews, choosing workout strategy. Post-GRG, these units operate under fair-treatment frameworks separating turnaround support from recovery profit incentives. Transfer in is a strong SICR indicator.

docs.title: Insolvency Service
docs.text: The government agency overseeing UK insolvency: it runs the Official Receiver service, regulates the IP profession, investigates director misconduct and publishes the official insolvency statistics — the canonical source for regime mix, sector patterns and failure rates used in BB credit and impairment analysis.

docs.title: Basel 3.1
docs.text: The UK's implementation of the final Basel III capital standards: revised standardised risk weights, constrained internal models, and an output floor. PRA near-final rules came in 2024; implementation was delayed in January 2025 to 1 January 2027, with the market-risk internal model approach following in 2028.

docs.title: SME supporting factor
docs.text: An EU-inherited Pillar 1 discount that scaled down capital risk weights on qualifying SME exposures, making small-business lending cheaper for banks to hold. Under UK Basel 3.1 it is removed from Pillar 1 from January 2027, offset by a firm-specific Pillar 2A SME lending adjustment.

docs.title: SME lending adjustment
docs.text: The PRA's firm-specific Pillar 2A offset introduced with Basel 3.1 to neutralise the aggregate capital impact of removing the SME supporting factor. Being supervisory and reviewable rather than automatic, it is less reliable for loan pricing than the Pillar 1 factor it replaces.

docs.title: Small Domestic Deposit Taker (SDDT)
docs.text: The PRA's simplified prudential regime for smaller, domestically focused UK banks and building societies, developed alongside Basel 3.1. It spares eligible challengers the full complexity of the new framework — shaping the capital economics of the specialist lenders now writing most SME flow.

docs.title: Bank Referral Scheme
docs.text: Statutory scheme (from November 2016) requiring major banks to refer declined SME finance applicants, with consent, to designated platforms — Funding Options, Funding Xchange, Alternative Business Funding, Business Finance Technology — that match them with alternative lenders. Reviewed in 2024–26; government opted against legislative overhaul in May 2026.

docs.title: Open finance
docs.text: The extension of open banking's data-sharing principles beyond payment accounts to savings, credit, investments and commercial products. The FCA is building the framework under 2026 legislation granting it rule-making powers, with commercial data expected to reshape SME credit assessment and monitoring.

docs.title: Commercial VRP
docs.text: Variable recurring payments extended beyond sweeping between own accounts to third-party billing — utilities, subscriptions, government. A 31-firm UK Payments Initiative scheme formed in late 2025, with first live payments from early 2026. VRPs already account for roughly 16% of open banking payment volumes.

docs.title: APP fraud
docs.text: Authorised push payment fraud: the victim is deceived into instructing a genuine payment to a fraudster. Since 7 October 2024, UK rules mandate reimbursement up to £85,000 within five business days, split 50/50 between sending and receiving firms. Scope covers consumers, micro-enterprises and charities — not larger business accounts.

docs.title: Private credit
docs.text: Non-bank lending by funds — direct lending, asset-based strategies — funded by institutional capital rather than deposits. Having absorbed much of leveraged lending, it is moving down into UK SME credit: non-banks and challengers wrote roughly 68% of the £68bn 2025 SME lending flow.

docs.title: BNPL (business)
docs.text: Buy-now-pay-later: short-term instalment credit at the point of sale. Consumer BNPL became FCA-regulated on 15 July 2026; B2B BNPL — pay-later terms embedded in trade checkouts by Kriya, Hokodo, iwocaPay — remains unregulated, growing toward an estimated US$16.5bn UK market, and largely invisible to credit bureaus.

docs.title: Embedded finance
docs.text: Credit, payments or insurance delivered inside a non-financial platform — accounting software, e-commerce checkouts, procurement portals — rather than through a bank channel. In UK SME finance it is displacing manual invoice finance, with regulated balance sheets (e.g. Allica–Kriya) increasingly funding fintech distribution.

docs.title: Refinancing wall
docs.text: The concentration of fixed-rate SME debt written in the ultra-low-rate 2020–21 window maturing across 2024–2027, forcing refinancing at materially higher rates. It transmits rate rises to borrower cash flow with a multi-year lag — so debt-service stress keeps building even while Bank Rate falls.
